entry.title: My Plans for Advent of Code - 2026
entry.content:
What is it?

Advent of Code is an annual set of Christmas-themed computer programming challenges that follow the story of the North Pole elves making necessary preparations for smooth festivity operations, unraveled day by day akin to how an Advent calendar is opened. It has been running since 2015. It was created by Eric Wastl (via Wikipedia).

How it works

For each day from the first day of December up until the 12th day, two puzzles are dropped, the goal being to solve those puzzles with any programming language of your choice in order to obtain the stars linked to that day's puzzles. The second puzzle for each day does not unlock until the first is solved.

There is no actual code upload for the solutions. You're only required to upload the actual answers you get from solving the puzzle.

The puzzles cover a wild variety of skill levels and are a fun way to put your problem-solving skills and programming experience to the test. I first came across Advent of Code in December 2024. I haven't completed the puzzle set for any year so far, but regardless I look forward to doing so this year.

2026

The puzzles begin on December 1st. I plan to write about my experience solving the puzzles and document the many exciting things I will learn along the way here on my blog. The website does have a leaderboard feature, where you can create a private leaderboard and invite your friends to join. At the same time, it discourages overly publicizing your leaderboard. These events are meant to be fun and cheerful, and a large leaderboard creates a competitive tension that strains that.

As with most things recently in the programming space, human efforts are slowly taking a back seat to AI-assisted or generated coding. I personally think it robs you of the ability to genuinely enjoy and learn from the puzzles, so I will not be using AI-generated code for my solutions.

I have a public GitHub repository where I keep my solutions for all the years, and you're welcome to go through it and learn how I approach the problems here. I implement my solutions in Python, Rust and Pylox, an experimental interpreted language I built while following the book Crafting Interpreters by Robert Nystrom.

Where to go from here

There is an incredibly active community on Reddit where users post guides, explainers and, most impressive to me, animated forms of their solutions to the puzzles. I will write about each day and its solution here on my blog. I really look forward to having fun and completing my first year of Advent of Code. If you would like to join my private leaderboard, you can send me a message on any of my socials.

Create an account and be ready - here

Merry Christmas ✨ in advance.

entry.title: Entanglement: The Experiment That Proved Einstein Wrong
entry.content:
Introduction

Einstein never accepted quantum mechanics as the final word. He was happy with its predictions; what he refused was the idea that a particle doesn't have definite properties until it's measured, the idea at the heart of the uncertainty principle. In 1935, with Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen, he wrote a paper arguing that quantum mechanics must be incomplete: there had to be hidden details it was leaving out.

For about thirty years this looked like a philosophical argument that could never be settled. Then in 1964, John Bell found a way to turn it into an experiment. The experiment has since been done, over and over, with steadily fewer loopholes. Einstein's picture lost. The 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics went to three of the people who did those experiments.

What I love about Bell's theorem is that the core of it is just counting. You can check it with a simulation and a bit of arithmetic, which is exactly what I'll do in this post.

TL;DR

  • Two entangled particles have perfectly linked measurement results, however far apart they are.
  • Einstein argued the results must be pre-set at the source, like a pair of gloves split into two boxes. That's a local hidden variable theory.
  • Bell showed that any such theory obeys a limit on how strongly the results can be correlated. In the CHSH version, a number called S can be at most 2.
  • Quantum mechanics predicts S up to 2√2 ≈ 2.83, and experiments agree. So the results can't have been pre-set by anything local.
  • It still can't be used to send messages faster than light.

Entanglement in one paragraph

Two particles can be prepared in a joint quantum state where neither has a definite value on its own, but their values are linked. A standard example is a pair of electrons in the singlet state: if you measure the spin of both along the same axis, you always get opposite answers. One up, one down. Which one is up is completely random, 50/50, but they're always opposite. This holds whether the electrons are a millimetre apart or on different continents.

The EPR argument: gloves in boxes

At first glance, perfect correlation isn't spooky at all. Take a pair of gloves, put one in each of two boxes without looking, and post one to Lagos and one to Tokyo. Open the box in Lagos, find a left glove, and you instantly know Tokyo has the right one. Nothing travelled between the boxes. The answer was decided when the gloves were packed.

Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen argued that entangled particles must work like this. If you can predict the result at Tokyo with certainty, without touching it, then that result must correspond to some element of reality that was there all along. Quantum mechanics doesn't include these pre-set values in its description, so it must be incomplete.

This view has two ingredients:

  1. Realism: the measurement results are determined in advance by properties the particles carry. Physicists call these hidden variables.
  2. Locality: what happens to one particle can't instantly affect the other. Nothing travels faster than light.

Together they make a local hidden variable theory. It sounds like common sense. Bell showed it makes a testable prediction, and that prediction is wrong.

Where the gloves analogy breaks: choosing the angle

The twist is that spin can be measured along any direction, and the measurer chooses.

Measure both electrons along the same axis and the results are always opposite. Measure them along axes at 90° and the results are completely uncorrelated. In between, quantum mechanics predicts the correlation follows a smooth cosine:

E(a, b) = −cos(a − b)

where E is the average of the product of the two results (+1 or −1 each), and a, b are the two measurement angles. E = −1 means always opposite, 0 means no relation, +1 means always the same.

A local hidden variable model can try to reproduce this. Each pair could carry a little instruction sheet saying what to answer for every possible angle. The question Bell asked is whether any instruction sheet can match that cosine. The answer is no.

The CHSH inequality

The most practical version of Bell's result came in 1969 from John Clauser, Michael Horne, Abner Shimony and Richard Holt, and it's known by their initials, CHSH.

Alice and Bob each have two measurement settings: Alice chooses a or a′, Bob chooses b or b′. They measure lots of pairs, choosing settings at random, and compute:

S = E(a, b) − E(a, b′) + E(a′, b) + E(a′, b′)

Here's why local hidden variables can't push |S| past 2. Suppose each pair carries pre-set answers A, A′ for Alice and B, B′ for Bob, all ±1. For one pair:

A·B − A·B′ + A′·B + A′·B′  =  A·(B − B′) + A′·(B + B′)

B and B′ are each ±1, so either they're equal, and B − B′ = 0 while B + B′ = ±2, or they're opposite, and it's the other way round. Either way, one bracket is 0 and the other is ±2, so the whole thing is exactly ±2. Average over any mix of pairs and you can't get beyond 2.

That's the whole proof. No quantum mechanics involved, only the assumption that the answers existed before the measurement and that Alice's choice can't change Bob's answer.

Quantum mechanics, with angles a = 0°, a′ = 90°, b = 45°, b′ = 135°, predicts:

|S| = 4 × cos(45°) = 2√2 ≈ 2.83

It breaks the limit. And 2√2 is the most any quantum system can reach, a bound found by Boris Tsirelson in 1980.

Simulating it in Python

Let's check both claims. The first source is a reasonable local hidden variable model: each pair leaves the source carrying a hidden angle, and each detector answers based only on its own setting and that angle. The second samples outcomes from quantum mechanics' predicted probabilities.

import math
import random

def local_pair(a: float, b: float) -> tuple[int, int]:
    """Local hidden variables: each pair leaves the source carrying a hidden angle."""
    hidden = random.uniform(0, 2 * math.pi)
    alice = 1 if math.cos(a - hidden) >= 0 else -1
    bob = -1 if math.cos(b - hidden) >= 0 else 1
    return alice, bob

def quantum_pair(a: float, b: float) -> tuple[int, int]:
    """Spin singlet: outcomes sampled from quantum mechanics' predicted probabilities."""
    alice = random.choice((1, -1))
    opposite = random.random() < math.cos((a - b) / 2) ** 2
    bob = -alice if opposite else alice
    return alice, bob

def correlation(source, a: float, b: float, trials: int = 200_000) -> float:
    total = 0
    for _ in range(trials):
        alice, bob = source(a, b)
        total += alice * bob
    return total / trials

def chsh(source) -> float:
    a, a2 = 0.0, math.radians(90)
    b, b2 = math.radians(45), math.radians(135)
    return (correlation(source, a, b) - correlation(source, a, b2)
            + correlation(source, a2, b) + correlation(source, a2, b2))

random.seed(7)
print(f"Local hidden variables: |S| = {abs(chsh(local_pair)):.3f}")
print(f"Quantum mechanics:      |S| = {abs(chsh(quantum_pair)):.3f}")
print(f"Bell's limit: 2, quantum maximum: 2√2 = {2 * math.sqrt(2):.3f}")
Local hidden variables: |S| = 1.997
Quantum mechanics:      |S| = 2.826
Bell's limit: 2, quantum maximum: 2√2 = 2.828

The hidden-angle model gets perfect anti-correlation at equal angles, just like the real thing. It even sits right at the limit of 2. But no matter how you tweak it, you can't get it past 2. You're welcome to try: change local_pair however you like, as long as Alice's answer only uses a and hidden, and Bob's only uses b and hidden.

Notice the cheat in quantum_pair: Bob's result is computed using both angles, a − b. That's the only way a classical program can reproduce quantum statistics. To fake entanglement classically, one side has to know the other side's setting.

The experiments

The prediction is clear. Testing it took decades of increasingly clever experiments, usually with pairs of polarisation-entangled photons rather than electrons:

  • 1972: John Clauser and Stuart Freedman at Berkeley ran the first test and found a violation of Bell's inequality, in agreement with quantum mechanics.
  • 1982: Alain Aspect's team in Paris switched the measurement settings while the photons were in flight, so no signal at light speed could tell one detector what the other had chosen.
  • 1998 onwards: Anton Zeilinger's group in Innsbruck and Vienna used random number generators and longer distances to close more gaps, and later used entanglement for quantum teleportation.

Sceptics pointed to loopholes. If detectors miss many photons, maybe the ones they catch are a biased sample (the detection loophole). If the detectors are close enough, maybe a signal could pass between them (the locality loophole). In 2015, three groups, at Delft, Vienna and NIST in Colorado, closed both loopholes in the same experiments. The Delft team used electrons in diamonds 1.3 km apart. The violation held.

In 2022, Aspect, Clauser and Zeilinger shared the Nobel Prize in Physics "for experiments with entangled photons, establishing the violation of Bell inequalities and pioneering quantum information science."

What it does and doesn't mean

Bell's theorem rules out local hidden variables. At least one of Einstein's two ingredients has to go:

  • Give up realism: the results really don't exist until measured. This is the mainstream reading.
  • Give up locality: there are hidden variables, but they're nonlocal, as in the pilot-wave interpretation, where the guiding wave connects distant particles instantly.

What it doesn't allow is faster-than-light communication. Look at Alice's results on their own: they're a random 50/50 sequence no matter what Bob does. The correlation only appears when Alice and Bob bring their records together and compare, which needs an ordinary, light-speed-limited channel. This is called the no-signalling theorem. Entanglement is a correlation, not a telephone.

Why it matters now

What started as an argument about the nature of reality has become engineering:

  • Quantum key distribution: Artur Ekert's 1991 protocol uses Bell tests to check that nobody has intercepted a key. If an eavesdropper interfered, the correlation would drop below the quantum value. China's Micius satellite has distributed entangled photons between ground stations over 1,000 km apart.
  • Quantum computing: entanglement between qubits is the resource that lets quantum algorithms outperform classical ones on some problems. The 2025 Nobel Prize went to John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis for the 1980s experiments showing quantum behaviour in superconducting circuits, the same kind of circuits many of today's quantum computers are built from.
  • Device-independent security: because a Bell violation can't be faked by local means, you can certify randomness or security without trusting the devices you bought.

Conclusion

Bell's theorem is one of the rare cases where a philosophical debate got settled by experiment:

  • Entangled particles show perfect correlations, which on their own could be explained by pre-set answers, like gloves in boxes.
  • But with changeable measurement angles, any local pre-set-answer theory obeys |S| ≤ 2, and the proof is a few lines of algebra.
  • Quantum mechanics predicts and experiments confirm |S| ≈ 2√2, with every major loophole closed since 2015.
  • Nature is not locally realistic, and yet still can't be used to signal faster than light.

Einstein was right that something about quantum mechanics is strange. He was wrong about which part. The strangeness isn't a gap in the theory; it's the way the world actually works.

entry.title: Introduction to Bytes in Rust. Part 1
entry.content:
Why you have probably never had to think about bytes

As a backend developer, most of my work sits at a high level of abstraction. I write handlers that take in structs, strings, vectors and the occasional custom enum, and return types that implement a particular trait.

Here is a handler from an Axum project:

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct Message {
    message: String,
}

async fn handler() -> Json<Message> {
    Json(Message {
        message: String::from("Hello World!"),
    })
}

No bytes in sight. You define a struct, derive a trait, return it, and you're done. Somewhere further down, that Json<Message> becomes a sequence of bytes on a network socket, but someone else already did that work for you.

That is true for most backend projects: the framework has built the plumbing, and your job is to combine those building blocks to solve business problems.

Things change when you go below that line and start building the blocks yourself: parsing a binary protocol, writing a file format, computing a checksum. There, understanding bytes stops being optional. I've been learning the fundamentals of bytes in Rust, and this post is my attempt to explain what I've understood to someone else. Explaining it is also the best test of whether I understand it.

Bits, bytes and the rest of the gang

When you send a friend an AI-generated meme, then at the lowest level that picture is nothing but a stream of bits travelling over a wire, a radio wave or a fibre-optic cable.

"Bit" is short for binary digit, and binary is a way of counting that uses only two digits: 0 and 1. In decimal, we count 0, 1, 2, ... 9 and then add a new digit to go higher (10). Binary works the same way, except it runs out of digits after 1, so it adds a new digit much sooner:

DecimalBinary
00
11
210
311
4100
5101
6110
7111
81000

Each position in a binary number is worth double the one to its right (1, 2, 4, 8, ...), just as decimal positions are worth 1, 10, 100, and so on. So 101 is 1×4 + 0×2 + 1×1 = 5.

Bytes

Think about how written language works. Letters are the basic symbols, but a single letter rarely means much on its own. Arrange them into words, then sentences, then paragraphs, and meaning appears.

Bits work similarly. A single bit carries very little, so we group them. A group of 8 bits is called a byte, and the byte is the basic unit that computers read, write and address in memory.

Eight bits can form 2⁸ = 256 different patterns, so a byte can represent any number from 0 to 255. (Not every piece of information is exactly 8 bits wide: a flag might use a single bit, and some formats pack fields across byte boundaries. But the byte is the unit everything is built on.)

Hexadecimal

Writing 11111111 every time you mean 255 is tedious and easy to get wrong, which is why we use hexadecimal, or "hex".

Hex is a base-16 counting system. It needs 16 digits, so after 0-9 it borrows the letters A-F (where A is 10 and F is 15). The useful part is that one hex digit corresponds to exactly 4 bits, so a byte is always exactly two hex digits:

BinaryHexDecimal
0000 00010x011
0100 00010x4165
1111 11110xFF255

The 0x prefix is just a marker meaning "this number is in hex". You'll see these constantly in low-level code. For example, 0x41 is 65, which happens to be the code for the letter A.

Why would anyone leave decimal for binary?

It does feel like unnecessary work. We already count comfortably in base 10, so why make computers use something harder to read?

The answer is that computers aren't built to be read by humans. They are built from electronic circuits, which work with physical signals. Telling apart two states, a high voltage and a low voltage, is easy and reliable. Telling apart ten distinct voltage levels is hard, because electrical noise is always present, and a small disturbance could turn a 7 into an 8.

Two states leave a wide margin for error, so circuits can be simple, fast and dependable. Switch between those two states billions of times a second, and you can express any information at all, as long as you agree on what the patterns mean. (Quantum computers work differently, but that's a story for another day.)

Bringing it down to Rust

Rust is a strongly typed language: every value has a type, and the compiler knows it at compile time. Often you write the type yourself as an annotation, but the compiler is smart enough to infer it in many cases.

The type for a single byte is u8: an unsigned 8-bit integer, holding values from 0 to 255.

let a: u8 = 65;
let b: u8 = 0x41;         // hex literal
let c: u8 = 0b0100_0001;  // binary literal (underscores are just for readability)
let d: u8 = b'A';         // byte literal: the ASCII code of 'A'

assert_eq!(a, b);
assert_eq!(b, c);
assert_eq!(c, d);

All four are the same value, written four different ways. A u8 can't hold 256 or more: let x: u8 = 256; fails to compile, and arithmetic that overflows (like 255u8 + 1) panics in debug builds.

Collections of bytes

You'll mostly work with bytes in groups, and Rust has three common shapes for that:

let fixed: [u8; 4] = [0x89, 0x50, 0x4E, 0x47]; // array: size fixed at compile time
let mut growable: Vec<u8> = Vec::new();         // Vec: grows as needed
growable.extend_from_slice(&fixed);

let view: &[u8] = &growable[1..3];              // slice: a borrowed view into bytes

That array is the start of every PNG file, the format your meme was probably sent in. The 0x50 0x4E 0x47 part spells PNG in ASCII.

Strings are bytes too

A Rust String or &str is really a sequence of bytes holding UTF-8 text, and you can look at them directly:

let s = "Hi!";
let bytes: &[u8] = s.as_bytes();
println!("{:?}", bytes);   // [72, 105, 33]

println!("{}", "é".len()); // 2

Note the last line: "é" is one character but two bytes, because UTF-8 uses more than one byte for characters outside basic ASCII. That's why len() on a string counts bytes, not characters.

To print numbers in hex or binary, use format specifiers:

println!("{:#04x} {:08b}", 65u8, 65u8); // 0x41 01000001

What's next

A u8 is easy, but most real data is bigger than one byte. A u32 takes four bytes, and then you face a question: which byte goes first?

let n: u32 = 0x1234_5678;
println!("{:02x?}", n.to_be_bytes()); // [12, 34, 56, 78]  big-endian
println!("{:02x?}", n.to_le_bytes()); // [78, 56, 34, 12]  little-endian

That's called endianness, and it's where I'll pick up in the next post.

entry.title: What I Learned (and Wish I'd Done Differently) at TechCabal's Moonshot
entry.content:
Why I Was There

A few months ago, I moved from Port Harcourt to Lagos with one mission: to tap into the city's tech ecosystem by attending events, meeting top talent, and getting the kind of exposure that could change my life.

Then, honestly, not much happened. My first months in Lagos were quiet. No events, no big introductions, just me, a laptop, and a plan that hadn't started yet.

That changed with TechCabal's Moonshot, my first tech event since the move. I loved it, but I also left with a list of things I wish I had done differently. This post covers both.

Arrival

I was so excited that I got to the National Theatre at about 8:30am, an hour and a half before the 10am start. It didn't matter. The place was already swarming with people, and from the energy around me, they were just as excited as I was.

Getting in was painless. I scanned my ticket, collected my tag, and walked in. No queues!

The hard part came after. From the start, I found the central hall confusing to navigate, and I spent my first stretch of the day just trying to work out where everything was.

The Sessions

The sessions are where Moonshot's tech focus really showed. This year's theme was "Courage & Conviction: Building for a New World," and three threads ran through the day for me: AI, the future of money, and building companies that last.

With talks running on several stages at once, I couldn't be everywhere, so I followed the topics closest to what I care about.

  • The State of AI in Nigeria: A panel on where Nigeria actually stands with AI, moderated by Dr. Olubayo Adekanmbi on the Big Tech and Enterprise Stage. It made me see AI as a data and infrastructure problem as much as a model problem. Without good local data, reliable compute, and trained people, the technology stays a demo. As someone with a data engineering background, that was the part of the stack I felt closest to.
  • Stablecoins & Monetary Sovereignty: Seun Lanlege's talk on the Future of Money Stage asked how stablecoins fit into a country's control over its own money. It changed how I think about payment rails. The technology can move value in seconds, but the harder questions are trust, regulation, and who gets to set the rules.
  • Forty Years A Tech Bro: What It Takes To Build Something That Lasts: Sir Demola Aladekomo, in conversation with Fu'ad Lawal, spoke about building across decades instead of funding cycles. It was a useful counterweight to the speed-obsessed side of tech: lasting companies are built on patience and fundamentals more than hype.
  • Building Africa's Workforce for the Global Economy: Joel Ogunsola's talk on the Workshop Stage was about preparing African talent to compete globally. It spoke directly to why I moved to Lagos. Opportunity tends to find people who put themselves in the room, and skills count for more when the right people can see them.

Hearing these ideas in one place made the ecosystem feel far more real than reading about it online ever had.

Walking the Exhibition Floor

If the sessions gave me ideas, the exhibition tour gave me exposure. Every company had a booth with banners, merchandise, and someone ready to explain what made their product different.

My favorite stop was Cloudflare. I'd been wondering whether they plan to support VPS-style machine provisioning for people who deploy on their cloud, so I asked. The answer was no. It wasn't what I'd hoped for, but getting a straight answer from the people who would know was worth the walk.

I also spoke with Liners, a software company that offers reviews and SEO boosting for African software products, and with a sales representative from Rexx, which describes itself as Africa's first AI-native banking solution. Other booths on my route included Grey, a fintech platform for cross-border payments, GoPaddi, an AI-powered platform for travel, tourism, hospitality, and business management, and Zikoko, a Nigerian digital and entertainment platform.

The People

Networking was the reason I moved, so I made a point of talking to people from different corners of tech. These are some of the new friends I made:

  • ID Inyang is a software engineer who builds practical applications for real-world problems. He specializes in backend development and system design, with a focus on software that is scalable, reliable, and efficient. Backend and system design is where I want to go deeper, so he's someone I plan to keep learning from.
  • Brian Ibekwe is a product manager at ReadPulse, where he works on building, improving, and growing the platform. Talking to someone who thinks in terms of users and growth gave me a useful contrast to my own more technical view of products.
  • Ninie: is a mobile videographer/content creator that is passionate about working with brands and individuals to bring their stories to life through engaging visual content
  • Emmanuel Obiabo works mostly with TypeScript and Rust, contributes to open source, and writes about whatever catches his interest. Much of his open-source work has been on blockchain projects in the Stellar ecosystem, and he is a long-time Linux user. You can read more about him here. His path through open source is one I'm curious to follow.
  • Bryan Benibo is a Founding Designer who helps startups build brands and intuitive digital products from scratch, blending creativity with strategy so the design drives real growth and customer engagement.
  • Marilyn is a UI/UX designer. Her portfolio includes TideReader, an AI-powered adaptive reading platform, Delve, a gamified language-learning platform, and Bubblr, a safe social media app for kids. Her case studies are a reminder that products live or die on design, and I'd love to work on something where engineering and design are in the same room.
  • Mauteen is a product design engineer who works where design meets engineering. That overlap is exactly what I want to understand better, so I'm glad we connected.
  • Eric is a creative software developer who builds mobile apps, backend systems, and web platforms end to end. He's a fellow builder, and the kind of person I'd happily build with.
  • Mary Adejumois product manager at Rex Microfinance Bank, where she owns the mobile app and website of the digital bank. She also built FindRyd, an AI-powered navigation app that gives delivery riders directions in landmarks instead of metres, taking it from 85 rider interviews to a tested prototype. A member of the Best Product Discovery Team in the 2026 PLA APM Fellowship, she writes things down until a team can build from them and tests the riskiest assumption first, which is a habit I want to pick up.

What I Wish I Had Done Differently

I'd call these small preparations, not big mistakes. But each one would have made the day easier.

1. Carry a personal card

Over and over, I did the same thing: pulled out my phone, found someone's LinkedIn or X handle, and typed mine in return. It was slow, it interrupted the conversation, and it only worked if both of us had the patience for it.

A personal card would have turned that into a two-second exchange. It doesn't have to be fancy: my name, what I do, and a QR code to my LinkedIn or GitHub. It would also give people something to remember me by when they leave a crowded venue with a bag of merchandise and a head full of names.

2. Wear something that starts conversations

Moonshot was a sea of similar tags and similar outfits, and it was hard to stand out. Branded wear, like a shirt or hoodie with my name, my role, or something I'm building, would have done some of the introducing for me. People would have had a reason to ask about it, and I wouldn't have had to open every conversation cold. It would also have made me easier to find again after a first meeting.

3. Plan my route through the day

I arrived early and still got lost in the halls. With sessions running on several stages at once, it's easy to drift toward whatever is closest instead of what matters. Next time, I'll bookmark my sessions the night before, note which stage each one is on, and leave gaps for the exhibition floor, so I'm choosing my time instead of just reacting to the crowd.

Final Thoughts

I moved to Lagos for moments like this one. Moonshot gave me sessions that sharpened my thinking, a floor full of companies to talk to, and a handful of people I'm glad to know. Next time, I'll show up with a card, an outfit that speaks for me, and a plan for the day. If you were at Moonshot, I'd love to hear what you'd do differently. And if this post was useful, share it with someone heading to their first tech event.

entry.title: Learning Technical Skills in the Age of SI
entry.content:
Introduction

Like many technical or skilled persons in the world at the moment, in the age of SI[1] it's becoming increasingly hard to feel special about the technical skill you possess, especially a skill like software mastery or software engineering. In recent times, I have had to come face to face with the reality that what made me special (with the hands in the air, defensively), in terms of my technical skills and experience in software programming, is largely not special anymore.

Now I have a real issue: Why should I invest real time like was done in the past, to gain mastery of topics that now feels very ephemeral? Why should I commit my weekend to understanding how Python's dictionary actually works under the hood and care about the details linked to open addressing, when I can generate more features far beyond my control in a product others could just as well vibe code?

At my most recent workplace (sad memories of my employed self), apart from the issues linked with lack of a concrete vision for the company's moat, I basically clocked out at some point, and just became a feature sprouting organism, attending demo after demo to wow always almost-at-the-verge-of-paying-clients. This was sad for me, because outside making a living with the skills I had acquired, I do genuinely love solving problems with the tools in my arsenal that actually ended up being used by people.

What was it really about for you?

The answer to this question would probably justify most people's stance on whether to bother committing to learning certain technical skills, if it was solely about implementing a feature, I guess you're better off moving fast and generating one with an LLM or some agent of sorts, but if it was really about mastering systems, understanding principles and unconsciously or consciously transferring those skills to other unrelated domains then the fear of being replaced should be less (notice how I said less, it doesn't go away). This does not invalidate the fear of losing out on a race of doing so much more with limited time and capital compared to any other time in history.

My Personal initial motivation

For me, it was always about mastery, I mean that mastery made my work easier, but I always loved the bits and bytes of it all, the quirks you had to get used to, and understand why they were, the rationales, the processes, it made committing to mastery very rewarding. All these contributed to building one's problem solving muscles across domains. For example I do this thing in my real life activities, where I try to do a lot of things concurrently in a beautifully scheduled way, mimicking asynchronous programming style: Like how I try to hack my chores and wait times on other activity by using those wait times to attend to other pending activities and I do it consciously and get excitement from being my own asynchronous runtime.

Is History Repeating itself?

I am sure a certain set of skilled person experienced things like this in the past, take for example, In the chess world, computers have practically perfected playing chess, and have since surpassed humans, but people still study it, and deep understanding separates good players from great ones. And that mastery is not any less valuable because it's beneath a computer's.

I think the same argument can be made for what is happening to software engineering and maths at this point in history, of course everyone can spin up a React App and get a well documented API powering it, but I believe it's a matter of time, before the mass hysteria dies off (this is actual wishful thinking) and people get bored of the AI hype. Is there a place of SI in work? of course, but I have accepted that mastery is personal and it does in fact reward more even outside of the specific domain of application.

Conclusion

I could be terribly wrong, man! I don't know the future, but this sounds quite reasonable, so if you're reading this from some distant day in the future and you laugh at my sheer misdirection on how things were going to go, I want you to know I too was open to the possibility that things happened in ways I could not have predicted. Soooo!! Do whatever makes you happy, and if that includes mastery of the internals of Fortran or memorizing factorials of a very large number, by all means go crazy. entry.title: The Uncertainty Principle Is Not About Clumsy Measurements
entry.content:
Introduction

Ask most people what Heisenberg's uncertainty principle says and you'll hear something like: "you can't measure a particle without disturbing it." To see an electron you have to bounce light off it, the light kicks it, and so you lose track of where it was going.

That explanation is intuitive, and Heisenberg himself used a version of it in 1927. It's also misleading. The uncertainty principle isn't a limit on our instruments. It's a statement about what a particle is. Even with perfect, gentle, impossible measuring tools, a particle simply does not have a precise position and a precise momentum at the same time.

In this post I want to make that idea feel obvious rather than mysterious. The trick is to think about waves. Then I'll use the principle to do something I find delightful: work out the size of a hydrogen atom in about ten lines of Python.

TL;DR

  • Quantum particles are described by waves, and momentum is the wavelength (p = h/λ).
  • A wave with a precise wavelength has to be spread out. A wave squeezed into a small region has to mix many wavelengths. That's not physics, it's a property of all waves.
  • So Δx · Δp ≥ ħ/2: the spread in position times the spread in momentum can't go below a fixed limit. No measurement required.
  • The same idea explains why electrons don't spiral into the nucleus, why there's zero-point energy, and why atoms are the size they are.

Start with waves, not particles

Forget quantum mechanics for a moment and think about sound.

A pure musical note, a single perfect frequency, is a sine wave that goes on and on. To be exactly one frequency, it has to last forever. If you cut it short, say a quick tap on a drum, the sound is localised in time, but it no longer has one pitch. A short click contains a whole spread of frequencies.

This is a mathematical fact about waves, usually expressed through the Fourier transform: any pulse can be built by adding together sine waves of different frequencies, and the shorter the pulse, the wider the range of frequencies you need. Engineers know this as the time–bandwidth product. It's why a radio signal that carries fast-changing data needs a wide frequency band, and it's something I first met in signals and systems classes, long before I connected it to quantum physics.

The same is true in space instead of time. A wave with a single, precise wavelength has to stretch across all of space. A wave packet confined to a small region has to be built from many different wavelengths.

Now add quantum mechanics

Here's the quantum ingredient, due to Louis de Broglie: a particle is described by a wave, and its momentum is tied to its wavelength:

p = h / λ

Put the two ideas together:

  • A particle with a precise momentum has a precise wavelength, so its wave is spread across all of space. Its position is completely undefined.
  • A particle with a precise position has a wave squeezed into a tiny region, which requires many wavelengths mixed together. Its momentum is completely undefined.
  • Anything in between is a trade-off.

That's the uncertainty principle. It's not that the particle has a definite position and momentum that we can't quite pin down. It's that a wave can't have both a sharp location and a sharp wavelength, and a quantum particle is that wave.

The formula

Made precise, the relationship is:

Δx · Δp ≥ ħ / 2
  • Δx is the spread (standard deviation) of position.
  • Δp is the spread of momentum.
  • ħ ("h-bar") is the reduced Planck constant, h / 2π ≈ 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.

The exact form with ħ/2 was proved in 1927 by Earle Kennard, shortly after Heisenberg's paper. The equality is reached only by one shape of wave packet: a Gaussian, the bell curve. Every other shape is more spread out.

Two notes worth making.

The spreads are about many repeated experiments. Prepare a million electrons in the same state. Measure position on half of them, momentum on the other half. The spreads in those two sets of results always obey the inequality. Each individual measurement can be as precise as your equipment allows. What you can't do is prepare a state where both sets of results come out sharp.

ħ is tiny. For a 1 gram marble whose position is known to within a micrometre, the minimum uncertainty in its velocity is about 5 × 10⁻²⁶ m/s. Your marble would take longer than the age of the universe to drift a millimetre. That's why you never notice this in everyday life. For an electron, with a mass about 10²⁷ times smaller, the effect is everything.

Why "measurement disturbs it" is the wrong picture

Heisenberg's original argument was the gamma-ray microscope: to locate an electron precisely, you need short-wavelength light, which carries a big momentum kick, which disturbs the electron's momentum.

That's a real effect, but it suggests the electron had a precise position and momentum before you interfered with it. Experiments say otherwise. The famous tests of Bell's theorem rule out any theory in which particles carry definite, pre-existing values for all their properties, if those values only depend on local influences. The uncertainty is in the particle, not in our clumsiness.

There's also an elegant way to see it from the double-slit experiment. Send a particle through a single narrow slit. Narrowing the slit pins down its sideways position (small Δx), and the particle's landing spot on the screen spreads out wider (large Δp). That's diffraction. No one is measuring anything at the slit. It's just a wave going through a gap.

Why atoms don't collapse

This is the part that made the uncertainty principle click for me.

Classical physics has an embarrassing problem with atoms. An electron orbiting a proton is an accelerating charge, and accelerating charges radiate. It should lose energy and spiral into the nucleus in about a hundred-billionth of a second. Every atom in the universe should have collapsed.

The uncertainty principle stops it. If the electron gets squeezed into a smaller region of size r, its momentum spread grows to roughly ħ / r, which means more kinetic energy, roughly ħ²/(2mr²). Meanwhile its electric potential energy falls as -ke²/r. The kinetic term grows faster as r shrinks, so there's a size where the total energy is lowest. That's the atom.

Let's find it:

HBAR = 1.054_571_8e-34     # reduced Planck constant, J·s
M_E = 9.109_383_7e-31      # electron mass, kg
KE2 = 2.307_077_6e-28      # e² / (4πε₀), J·m
EV = 1.602_176_6e-19       # joules per electron-volt

def energy(r: float) -> float:
    """Total energy of an electron squeezed into a region of size r."""
    kinetic = HBAR ** 2 / (2 * M_E * r ** 2)   # from Δp ≈ ħ / r
    potential = -KE2 / r                       # attraction to the proton
    return kinetic + potential

# Scan sizes from 0.01 to 5 ångström and keep the one with the lowest energy
sizes = [i * 1e-13 for i in range(100, 50_000)]
best = min(sizes, key=energy)

print(f"Most stable size: {best * 1e10:.3f} Å")
print(f"Energy there:     {energy(best) / EV:.2f} eV")
for r in (0.1e-10, 0.25e-10, best, 2e-10):
    print(f"  r = {r * 1e10:5.2f} Å -> E = {energy(r) / EV:8.2f} eV")
Most stable size: 0.529 Å
Energy there:     -13.61 eV
  r =  0.10 Å -> E =   237.00 eV
  r =  0.25 Å -> E =     3.36 eV
  r =  0.53 Å -> E =   -13.61 eV
  r =  2.00 Å -> E =    -6.25 eV

0.529 ångström is the Bohr radius, the textbook size of a hydrogen atom. And −13.6 eV is exactly the measured ground-state energy of hydrogen: the energy it takes to ionise it.

I'll confess that landing on both numbers exactly is partly luck: Δp ≈ ħ/r is a rough estimate, and a different choice of constant would shift the answer by a factor of order one. But the point stands. Squeeze the electron and its kinetic energy blows up (look at the 237 eV at 0.1 Å). The uncertainty principle is literally what gives matter its size. It's the reason you don't fall through the floor.

Zero-point energy

The same argument says a quantum system can never be perfectly still. A particle sitting motionless at the bottom of a valley would have precise position and zero momentum, which is forbidden. So even at absolute zero, there's some unavoidable jiggling, called zero-point energy.

It has real consequences. It's why helium never freezes at normal pressure, even at absolute zero: helium atoms are so light and so weakly attracted to each other that their zero-point motion is enough to stop them locking into a crystal. You have to squeeze it to about 25 atmospheres to make solid helium.

Other pairs

Position and momentum aren't the only pair with this trade-off. In general, any two quantities whose quantum operators don't commute have one. The best known others:

  • Spin along different axes. An electron can't have a definite spin both up–down and left–right. Measure one and the other becomes completely random.
  • Energy and time, in a slightly different sense: a state that only lasts a short time has a spread of energies. That's why short-lived excited states emit light with a broader range of colours, and why unstable particles have a "width" in their mass.

Conclusion

The uncertainty principle is more natural, and more fundamental, than its popular description suggests:

  • It comes from waves: a sharp position and a sharp wavelength can't coexist, and in quantum mechanics wavelength is momentum.
  • Δx · Δp ≥ ħ/2 is about the state of the particle, not the quality of the measuring tools.
  • It's not a nuisance at the edge of physics. It sets the size of atoms, gives every system a zero-point energy, and keeps helium liquid at absolute zero.

The next question is the one that troubled Einstein most: if a particle doesn't have definite properties until they're measured, what happens when two particles share a state and are measured far apart? That's entanglement, and it gets its own post.

entry.title: Nuclear Fusion: Why Building a Star on Earth Is So Hard
entry.content:
Introduction

There is an old joke that fusion power is thirty years away, and always will be. It's been told for so long that it's become part of the subject. And yet the physics is not in doubt: every second, the Sun fuses around 600 million tonnes of hydrogen, and has been doing it for 4.6 billion years. Fusion obviously works. The question is why it's so devilishly hard to do it here.

This is the third post in a small series. In the first, I explained the binding energy curve, and in the second, how fission climbs it from the heavy side. Fusion climbs it from the light side, and it's the bigger prize. You don't need to have read either post to follow this one.

TL;DR

  • Fusing light nuclei, like hydrogen isotopes into helium, releases energy because helium is far more tightly bound. Per kilogram, it beats fission by about four times.
  • The obstacle is the Coulomb barrier: nuclei are positively charged and repel each other, so you need them extremely hot (~150 million °C) to get close enough.
  • Even then, they only fuse thanks to quantum tunnelling.
  • A power plant needs hot enough plasma, dense enough, held for long enough: the Lawson criterion. Magnetic confinement (tokamaks, stellarators) and inertial confinement (lasers) are two different bets on how to get there.
  • In late 2022, the US National Ignition Facility got more fusion energy out of a target than the lasers put in, a first, and it has since improved that. Nobody has yet produced net electricity.

The reaction everyone is chasing

The Sun fuses ordinary hydrogen, but slowly (more on that below). Every serious fusion power design on Earth uses a faster reaction between two heavier hydrogen isotopes, deuterium (one proton, one neutron) and tritium (one proton, two neutrons):

²H + ³H  →  ⁴He (3.5 MeV) + n (14.1 MeV)

Total energy: 17.6 MeV per reaction. The helium nucleus is the star of the binding energy curve, unusually tightly bound for its size, and dropping into that state releases a lot of energy.

Per reaction, 17.6 MeV is less than the ~200 MeV of a uranium fission. But only five nucleons are involved instead of 236. Per kilogram of fuel, D-T fusion releases about 340 terajoules, roughly four times more than fission and around ten million times more than burning coal.

Notice that four-fifths of the energy leaves with the neutron. Neutrons have no charge, so no magnetic field can hold them. They fly straight out of the plasma and into the walls. That fact quietly shapes almost every fusion engineering problem, and I'll come back to it.

The real enemy: the Coulomb barrier

Here is the core difficulty. The strong nuclear force that makes fusion possible only reaches about a femtometre or two. To feel it, two nuclei have to almost touch. But both nuclei are positively charged, and the electric repulsion between them grows stronger the closer they get.

For deuterium and tritium, the repulsion peaks at around 0.4 MeV just before the strong force takes over. That's the Coulomb barrier: a hill of electric potential energy the nuclei have to climb.

The obvious way to give particles energy is to heat them. In a gas, temperature is a measure of the particles' average kinetic energy. So how hot would deuterium and tritium need to be to have an average energy of 0.4 MeV? About 4.6 billion kelvin. The core of the Sun is about 15 million kelvin, three hundred times cooler. By classical physics alone, the Sun shouldn't shine.

Quantum tunnelling to the rescue

Classical physics says a particle without enough energy to get over a hill simply can't. Quantum mechanics disagrees. A particle is described by a wave, and that wave doesn't stop dead at a barrier. It decays inside it, and if the barrier is thin enough, some of the wave leaks out the other side. The particle has a small but real probability of appearing beyond a barrier it couldn't classically climb. This is quantum tunnelling.

The tunnelling probability rises steeply with energy: faster nuclei face a thinner, lower part of the barrier. Meanwhile, in a hot gas, very few particles are fast. Their energies follow a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, which drops off exponentially at high energy.

Multiply these two together, "plenty of particles but bad tunnelling" at low energy and "great tunnelling but almost no particles" at high energy, and you get a narrow window where most fusion actually happens. This is the Gamow peak, named after George Gamow who first worked out tunnelling for nuclear decay in 1928.

Here's a small script that computes where that peak sits:

import math

ALPHA = 1 / 137.036          # fine-structure constant
U_TO_KEV = 931_494.0         # atomic mass unit in keV/c^2
K_B = 8.617e-8               # Boltzmann constant in keV per kelvin

def gamow_peak(Z1, Z2, m1, m2, temperature_k):
    """Return (Gamow energy, thermal energy kT, most likely fusion energy), all in keV."""
    reduced_mass = m1 * m2 / (m1 + m2) * U_TO_KEV
    e_gamow = 2 * reduced_mass * (math.pi * ALPHA * Z1 * Z2) ** 2
    kT = K_B * temperature_k
    peak = (e_gamow * kT ** 2 / 4) ** (1 / 3)
    return e_gamow, kT, peak

cases = {
    "p + p in the Sun's core (15.7 million K)": (1, 1, 1.00728, 1.00728, 15.7e6),
    "D + T in a reactor (150 million K)": (1, 1, 2.01355, 3.01550, 150e6),
}

for label, (Z1, Z2, m1, m2, T) in cases.items():
    e_g, kT, peak = gamow_peak(Z1, Z2, m1, m2, T)
    print(f"{label}\n  kT = {kT:.2f} keV, Gamow peak = {peak:.1f} keV ({peak / kT:.1f} x kT)")
p + p in the Sun's core (15.7 million K)
  kT = 1.35 keV, Gamow peak = 6.1 keV (4.5 x kT)
D + T in a reactor (150 million K)
  kT = 12.93 keV, Gamow peak = 36.7 keV (2.8 x kT)

Even in a fusion reactor, the nuclei that actually fuse carry around 37 keV: a tenth of the height of the barrier. Every single fusion reaction, in the Sun and in our machines, is a tunnelling event.

Why the Sun gets away with it, and we can't

The Sun has two huge advantages. It has gravity to hold its fuel together for free, and it has time. Its core is so vast and dense that even a pitifully slow reaction rate adds up to an enormous output.

And it really is slow. The first step of the Sun's proton–proton chain needs one proton to turn into a neutron mid-collision, via the weak nuclear force, which almost never happens. A given proton in the Sun's core waits, on average, billions of years before it fuses. The power density in the solar core is only around 275 watts per cubic metre, comparable to a compost heap. The Sun is bright because it is big, not because it is intense.

On Earth we have neither the gravity nor the size. So we compensate in two ways:

  1. Use a much easier reaction. D-T needs no weak-force miracle. Its cross-section is around 10²⁴ times larger than proton–proton fusion at similar energies.
  2. Run much hotter than the Sun. Around 150 million kelvin, ten times the temperature of the solar core, which is where D-T's reaction rate is near its best per unit of pressure.

At those temperatures, electrons are stripped from their nuclei and the fuel becomes a plasma, a soup of charged particles. No material can touch it. Hold it in a container and the plasma cools instantly while the container vaporises.

The Lawson criterion

In 1955, the engineer John Lawson asked the question in its most practical form: when does a fusion plasma produce more energy than it loses? The modern version for D-T comes down to the triple product:

n × T × τ_E  ≳  3 × 10²¹  keV·s/m³
  • n: the density of fuel ions. More particles, more collisions.
  • T: the temperature. Hot enough to sit near D-T's sweet spot.
  • τ_E: the energy confinement time. How long the plasma holds its heat before losing it.

If the triple product clears that bar, the energy from the helium nuclei (which, being charged, stay in the plasma) is enough to keep the plasma hot without any outside heating. That's ignition: a self-sustaining burn, like a fire that no longer needs a match.

Every fusion approach is a strategy for maximising that product, and they fall into two camps.

Two ways to bottle a star

Magnetic confinement: low density, long time

Charged particles in a magnetic field spiral along the field lines. Bend the field lines into a closed loop, and in principle the particles go round forever without touching a wall.

A simple ring of field doesn't quite work. The field is stronger on the inside of the ring than the outside, and particles drift out. The fix is to twist the field lines as they go round, so each particle samples both sides and the drifts cancel. There are two ways to do the twisting:

  • The tokamak, a Soviet design from the 1950s, drives a large electric current through the plasma itself, and the current's own magnetic field supplies the twist. It's the most advanced design, but that current is a source of instabilities. The worst are disruptions, where the plasma loses confinement in milliseconds and dumps its energy into the walls.
  • The stellarator builds the twist into the external magnets, which are wound into bizarre three-dimensional shapes. No plasma current is needed, so it's naturally steady and calmer, but the magnets are much harder to design and build. Germany's Wendelstein 7-X is the flagship.

Magnetic confinement works with thin plasma, around a millionth of the density of air, held for seconds or longer. The European JET tokamak in the UK set the record for total fusion energy in a single pulse, 69 megajoules over about five seconds, in its final campaign in 2023 before it shut down. ITER, the enormous international tokamak under construction in southern France, is meant to produce ten times more fusion power than the heating it receives. Its schedule has slipped repeatedly; under its 2024 baseline, deuterium–tritium operation isn't due until the late 2030s.

The most interesting recent shift is in magnets. A tokamak's performance rises steeply with magnetic field strength. New high-temperature superconducting tape (REBCO) can produce much stronger fields than the superconductors ITER uses, which means a reactor could get the same performance in a far smaller machine. Commonwealth Fusion Systems demonstrated a 20-tesla magnet built this way in 2021 and is building a compact tokamak called SPARC around it, aiming to show net energy gain in the plasma later this decade.

Inertial confinement: high density, tiny time

The other camp turns the problem inside out. Instead of holding a thin plasma for a long time, crush a speck of fuel to enormous density and let it burn in the instant before it flies apart. The fuel's own inertia is the "container".

The National Ignition Facility (NIF) in California does this with 192 lasers. They fire into a small gold cylinder called a hohlraum, about the size of a pencil eraser, turning the laser light into X-rays. Those X-rays blast the surface off a peppercorn-sized capsule of frozen D-T, and the recoil compresses the fuel inward like a rocket in reverse. For a few billionths of a second the centre reaches over 100 million kelvin and densities around a hundred times that of lead.

On 5 December 2022, NIF delivered 2.05 MJ of laser energy to the target and got 3.15 MJ of fusion energy back. For the first time, a controlled fusion experiment produced more energy than was put into the fuel. NIF has repeated and beaten that since, reaching yields of around 8.6 MJ in 2025.

Gain: the fine print

Headlines about "net energy" need careful reading, and this is where my engineering side wants to be pedantic. There are several different ratios people call Q:

MeasureWhat it comparesStatus
Scientific gainFusion energy out ÷ energy delivered to the fuelAbove 1 at NIF since 2022
Facility gainFusion energy out ÷ energy drawn from the grid to run the machineFar below 1
Engineering gainElectricity sold ÷ electricity usedNot yet attempted

NIF's lasers draw around 300 MJ from the grid to deliver those 2 MJ of laser light, because the lasers are about 1% efficient (they were built in the 1990s for weapons research, not efficiency). And a power plant would then need to convert fusion heat to electricity at maybe 40%, and fire several shots per second, not one a day. The 2022 result was a genuine scientific milestone. It's not yet a power plant, nor close to one.

The problems after ignition

Getting the plasma to burn is the famous problem. Turning that into a power station brings a second list, and these are mostly materials and engineering problems, not physics:

  • The neutrons. Those 14.1 MeV neutrons carry 80% of the energy and hammer the walls, knocking atoms out of place and making the structure brittle and mildly radioactive over time. We still need materials that can survive years of it. A dedicated test facility (IFMIF-DONES in Spain) is being built specifically for this.
  • Tritium. Tritium is radioactive with a half-life of 12.3 years, so there's almost none in nature, and the world's civilian stockpile is only a few tens of kilograms. A reactor would have to breed its own by surrounding the plasma with a lithium blanket, where neutrons do ⁶Li + n → ³H + ⁴He. Breeding more tritium than you burn, reliably, has never been demonstrated.
  • The exhaust. Heat leaving the plasma is funnelled onto a component called the divertor, which faces heat fluxes comparable to a spacecraft re-entering the atmosphere, continuously.
  • Staying on. A power plant needs to run steadily for months. Tokamaks have to manage instabilities, and laser plants would need to make, place and hit hundreds of thousands of precision targets every day, cheaply.

Why bother?

Because the payoff is extraordinary, and the downsides compared with fission are small:

  • Fuel. Deuterium can be extracted from seawater, about one in every 6,400 hydrogen atoms. Lithium for breeding tritium is plentiful. There is fuel for millions of years.
  • No runaway. There's no chain reaction. A fusion plasma is so hard to sustain that any fault makes it go out. The total fuel in the chamber at any moment is around a gram.
  • No long-lived waste. The helium product is harmless. The reactor structure becomes radioactive from the neutrons, but with the right materials that decays over decades to a century, not millennia.
  • No carbon, and a power station that runs regardless of weather, unlike wind and solar.

Conclusion

Fusion is hard for one reason that sits on top of everything else: positively charged nuclei don't want to get close to each other, and the only way past that is to make them so hot no material can hold them. The rest of the story follows:

  • D-T fusion releases 17.6 MeV per reaction and about four times more energy per kilogram than fission.
  • Nuclei only fuse by quantum tunnelling through the Coulomb barrier, even at 150 million kelvin.
  • Lawson's triple product, density × temperature × confinement time, is the scorecard every machine is judged by.
  • Scientific breakeven has happened, at NIF in 2022, but engineering breakeven, with real electricity, hasn't.

I've come away from writing this series more optimistic than I expected. The 30-year joke used to be funny because nobody had crossed a single real milestone. That's no longer true. There's still a long engineering road between "it works" and "it's on the grid", but for the first time, it's an engineering road.

entry.title: Common Gotchas When Working with Rust as a Python Developer
entry.content:
Transitioning from Python to Rust can present a myriad of unexpected challenges for developers. By identifying these common gotchas and understanding the nuances of Rust’s design philosophy, you can streamline your learning curve and develop more efficient code. In this guide, I’ll detail my experiences with the Rust programming language and provide illustrative examples to help ease your journey.

TL;DR;

Be mindful of specific Rust behaviors, such as explicit flushing of standard output, understanding ownership and borrowing, and mastering error handling.

Table of Contents

  • 1. Explicit Call to Flush Standard Output
  • 2. Understanding Ownership and Borrowing
  • 3. Error Handling: Comparisons between Rust and Python
  • 4. Differences in Concurrency Models
  • 5. Memory Management: Safe and Unsafe Rust
  • 6. Performance Challenges and Optimization Tips
  • 7. Conclusion
  • 8. Technical Deep-Dive Sections
  • 8.1 Advanced Ownership and Borrowing
  • 8.2 In-Depth Error Handling Techniques
  • 8.3 Concurrency Control in Depth
  • 9. Summary and Further Reading

1. Explicit Call to Flush Standard Output

When creating command-line applications, developers used to Python’s straightforward input function may face puzzling output behavior in Rust. The simple Python command below is familiar for prompting user input:

user_input = input("Enter your name: ")

This line effectively handles output and input seamlessly. However, when converting this to Rust, you may encounter unexpected behavior:

let mut user_input = String::new();
print!("Enter your name: ");
io::stdin().read_line(&mut user_input).unwrap();

Upon execution, the prompt may not display until after the user enters their input, making it appear unresponsive. This behavior stems from Rust’s output buffering in the context of the print! macro.

What’s Missing

The oversight here is that Rust does not automatically flush standard output when using the print! macro. For immediate visibility, developers must incorporate an explicit flush:

let mut user_input = String::new();
print!("Enter your name: ");
io::stdout().flush().unwrap(); // Flush the output to show the prompt immediately
io::stdin().read_line(&mut user_input).unwrap();

Practical Tips:

  • Always remember to include use std::io::{self, Write}; at the top of your Rust file if you use flushing methods.
  • Create a reusable helper function to wrap print! and flush calls to maintain consistency and improve code readability.

2. Understanding Ownership and Borrowing

Rust’s ownership model, rooted in ensuring memory safety without a garbage collector, can be one of the most challenging paradigm shifts for Python developers. In Python, it’s common to pass around variables without strict ownership rules. In Rust, however, understanding these principles can significantly affect your code’s safety and performance.

Ownership Rules

The essence of Rust’s ownership system includes:

  • One Owner at a Time: Each value in Rust has a single owner at any point.
  • Dropping Values: When the owner goes out of scope, Rust automatically calls the drop method to handle memory cleanup, thus preventing memory leaks.

Consider this Rust example demonstrating ownership transfer:

fn main() {
    let s1 = String::from("Hello");
    let s2 = s1; // s1’s ownership is transferred to s2
    // println!("{}", s1); // This will NOT compile; s1 is now invalid
}

Borrowing: Safe and Mutable References

To enable functions to access data without taking ownership, Rust introduces borrowing. There are two forms of borrowing:

  • Immutable References: Denoted by &value, allowing multiple references simultaneously.
  • Mutable References: Denoted by &mut value, permitting only one mutable reference at a time—thereby preventing data races.

Example: Borrowing

fn main() {
    let s1 = String::from("Hello");
    let len = calculate_length(&s1); // Borrowing s1 immutably
    println!("Length of '{}' is {}.", s1, len);
}

fn calculate_length(s: &String) -> usize {
    s.len() // Borrowing does not take ownership
}

This code illustrates how ownership and borrowing ensure safe access to memory, eliminating dangling pointers and data races.

Practical Tips:

  • Use ownership transfers judiciously to maintain performance; passing by reference often helps avoid excessive copying of data.
  • Familiarize yourself with Rust’s lifetime annotations to guide the borrowing system in complex scenarios—especially when dealing with multiple references.

3. Error Handling: Comparisons between Rust and Python

Rust’s approach to error handling is fundamentally different from Python’s exception system. Developers coming from Python, used to catching errors via try and except, may find Rust's explicit error handling both enlightening and demanding.

Rust’s Result Type

The Result<T, E> enum signifies outcomes that may succeed (type T) or fail (type E). This encourages handling errors explicitly at compile time:

use std::fs::File;
use std::io::{self, Read};

fn main() -> Result<(), io::Error> {
    // Opening a non-existent file will trigger an error
    let mut file = File::open("hello.txt")?; // Propagates error
    let mut content = String::new();
    file.read_to_string(&mut content)?;
    Ok(())
}

Using the ? operator provides a concise mechanism for error propagation; if an error occurs, it exits the function immediately.

Comparing with Python

In Python:

try:
    with open("hello.txt") as f:
        data = f.read()
except FileNotFoundError as e:
    print("File not found:", e)

This utilizes exception handling elegantly, enabling clearer control flow, but potentially obscuring some error states.

Key Takeaways

Rust compels developers to handle errors, enhancing robustness but injecting verbosity compared to Python’s simpler exception handling approach. Each potential error must be considered in Rust, leading to clearer, more maintainable code.

Practical Tips:

  • Leverage crates like anyhow for error handling that simplifies error definitions and captures more context on errors.
  • Establish custom error types with the thiserror crate to enhance clarity when logging and debugging.
  • Write unit tests to cover various error scenarios, which functions can produce, reinforcing the significance of explicit error handling.

4. Differences in Concurrency Models

Rust introduces a unique model for concurrency that guarantees the absence of data races at compile time, diverging significantly from Python’s Global Interpreter Lock (GIL).

Safe Concurrency in Rust

Using Mutex, Arc, and other synchronization primitives, Rust allows for safe data access across threads. Here's an example:

use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::thread;


fn main() {
    let counter = Arc::new(Mutex::new(0)); // Shared mutable state initialization
    let mut handles = vec![];
    for _ in 0..10 {
        let counter_clone = Arc::clone(&counter);
        let handle = thread::spawn(move || {
            let mut num = counter_clone.lock().unwrap(); // Safely lock the mutex
            *num += 1; // Mutable access
        });
        handles.push(handle);
    }
    for handle in handles {
        handle.join().unwrap(); // Wait for threads to complete
    }
    println!("Result: {}", *counter.lock().unwrap()); // Final count
}

Python’s GIL

In Python, threading is limited by the GIL, allowing only one thread to execute bytecode at a time. This presents challenges for CPU-bound applications, limiting developers when attempting to achieve better scalability.

Practical Tips:

  • Utilize Rust’s concurrency features, such as rayon, for more straightforward parallel data processing without manual thread management.
  • When translating Python code to Rust, assess if operations can be concurrent and leverage Rust’s concurrency abstractions for efficiency.

5. Memory Management: Safe and Unsafe Rust

Memory safety and management are core aspects of Rust’s design philosophy, emphasizing prevention of the common pitfalls found in many programming languages, including Python.

Safe Rust

The majority of Rust code adheres to “safe” coding practices, where the compiler enforces ownership rules and ensures no data is accessed incorrectly. This minimizes issues such as dereferencing null pointers and ensuring memory leaks do not occur.

Unsafe Rust

For certain performance-sensitive or system-level development, developers may employ unsafe code blocks. This provides flexibility to opt out of Rust's safety checks when necessary:

let r: *const i32 = &10; // Creating a raw pointer
unsafe {
    println!("{}", *r); // Dereferencing a raw pointer
}

Utilizing unsafe features allows manipulation of memory in powerful ways; however, employing unsafe code should always be approached with caution.

Practical Tips:

  • Review crates such as unsafe-code-guidelines to further your understanding of best practices when working with unsafe code.
  • Regularly evaluate whether your code can accomplish needs without unsafe blocks; strive to keep unsafe code isolated and manageable.

6. Performance Challenges and Optimization Tips

Rust’s capabilities are often celebrated for their performance benefits, yet to fully realize these advantages, a comprehensive approach to optimization is essential.

Performance Optimization Tips:

  1. Avoid Unnecessary Cloning: Instead of relying on cloning structures, utilize references whenever feasible. This reduces overhead and enhances performance in tight loops.
fn process_data(data: &Vec<i32>) {
    // Efficient handling of data without cloning
    // Perform operations directly on the data
}
  1. Profile Your Code: Utilize profiling tools such as cargo flamegraph or cargo bench for pinpointing performance bottlenecks. Profiling provides insights into where optimizations can save processing time.
  2. Utilize Smart Pointers: Use smart pointers, including Rc, Arc, and RefCell, to manage complex data ownership situations. For straightforward heap allocations, Box is a great choice.
  3. Opt For Idiomatic Rust Before Optimizing: Start with writing intuitive and maintainable code. Only engage in optimization when profiling reveals specific performance concerns to address.

Example of Optimized Code:

use std::collections::HashMap;

fn count_word_frequencies(words: &Vec<String>) -> HashMap<String, i32> {
    let mut frequency_map = HashMap::<String, i32>::new();
    for word in words {
        *frequency_map.entry(word.clone()).or_insert(0) += 1; // Increment frequency count
    }
    frequency_map
}

7. Technical Deep-Dive Sections

7.1 Advanced Ownership and Borrowing

Ownership and borrowing mechanics bear deeper investigation, particularly when applied to advanced data structures, including:

  • Complex Ownership Scenarios: The interactions between ownership in structs and enums and how lifetime annotations help maintain correctness.
  • Dynamic Borrowing: Secrets of borrowing across function calls, especially within closures, and the implications of mutable borrowing with respect to data access.

7.2 In-Depth Error Handling Techniques

Delve deeper into Rust’s error processing:

  • Creating Custom Error Types: Instruction for establishing distinct error types with enums and using the thiserror crate for ease of error propagation.
  • Handling Errors Gracefully: Strategies for managing complex error chains and ensuring the implementation remains user-friendly.

7.3 Concurrency Control in Depth

Concurrency in Rust is vital for building efficient applications:

  • Advanced Synchronization Primitives: Discover the uses of RwLock and Condvar, the contexts for their application, and trade-offs between performance and safety.
  • Async Programming in Rust: Exploration of asynchronous paradigms, including async/await, futures, and how to integrate them into the existing Rust infrastructure seamlessly.

8. Summary and Further Reading

This guide presents insights into common challenges developers face when migrating from Python to Rust, accentuating the differences in ownership, error management, and concurrency.

To extend your understanding, consider these resources:

  • The Rust Programming Language Book
  • Articles detailing Rust’s ownership model
  • Discussions focused on Asynchronous Programming

entry.title: Stop Writing Manual Validation: Master Pydantic
entry.content:
Introduction

Validation is a crucial part of any software that collects data from users or other external sources. This ensures that the data used in your program or application remains correct and well-structured. Serialization, which is the process of converting data from one format to another for transmission or storage, is also essential to ensure that we use the best data format for the right scenario (for example, using JSON for transmission and objects for storage in a database).

Pydantic is a library in the Python ecosystem that elegantly solves both use cases. To benefit greatly from the content of this article, it is assumed that you have familiarity with Python programming and a basic understanding of Object-Oriented Programming in Python.

Why Pydantic

Understanding Data Validation in Traditional Python

Before diving into Pydantic code, let’s explore how data validation can be handled for a practical scenario in plain, regular Python. Assume we have a software application for students in a university to register their courses for the semester.

# A class to store student data; this can be an instance of a record in the database
class Student:
    def __init__(self, name: str, email: str, year: int):
        self.name = name
        self.email = email
        self.year = year
        self.courses = set()

    def add_course(self, course: str):
        self.courses.add(course)
        return True
    def remove_course(self, course: str):
        self.courses.remove(course)
        return True


# Function to handle student registration
def register_student(name: str, email: str, year: int):
    return Student(name, email, year)

This is a simple way to represent a student record in our application, allowing for the storage and manipulation of student data through methods like adding or removing courses. However, validation for attributes like year can become intricate and verbose.

# Adding validation with an updated function version
def register_student_v2(name: str, email: str, year: int):
    if year not in range(1, 7):  # from 1 to 6, 7 is not included
        raise ValueError("Student Year must be between 1 and 6 years")
    return Student(name, email, year)

try:
    james = register_student_v2(name="James Okon", email="james@mail.com", year=1)
    grace = register_student_v2(name="Grace Mabel", email="grace@gmail.com", year=2)
    brian = register_student_v2(name="Brian Obot", email="brianobot9@gmail.com", year=1000)
except ValueError as err:
    print(f"Failed to register student because: {err}")

This illustrates how we incorporate validation for year, ensuring it meets predetermined requirements. However, adding validation checks for other properties requires additional verbose code, leading to repetitive structures.

Why To Use Pydantic?

Enter Pydantic. Here are some compelling reasons why Pydantic is an excellent option for validating and serializing data:

  1. Performance: Pydantic’s core validation logic is implemented in Rust; as a result, it stands out as one of the fastest data validation libraries for Python.
  2. Type Hints Powered Schema Validation: The schema that Pydantic uses to validate data is generally defined using Python type annotations/hints.
  3. Serialization: Pydantic excels at data serialization, crucial when converting data for network transfer or file storage.
  4. Strict Mode and Data Coercion: Pydantic attempts to coerce incorrect data into the right type by default, converting entries like numeric strings to integers as appropriate.
  5. Customization: Custom validation logic fits unique use cases seamlessly within Pydantic’s framework.
  6. Extensive Use in Big Projects: Many significant projects, especially in AI, leverage Pydantic, making it an essential skill for a Python developer.

Introduction to Pydantic

Pydantic is the most widely used data validation library for Python. It allows users to define validation and serialization rules through type annotations, enabling robust data management practices.

Basic Usage Example

Let’s revisit the student registration example but utilize Pydantic for validation.

from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, EmailStr, ValidationError

class Student(BaseModel):
    name: str
    email: EmailStr
    year: Annotated[int, Field(ge=1, le=6)]
try:
    james = Student(name="James Okon", email="james@mail.com", year=1)
    grace = Student(name="Grace Mabel", email="grace@gmail.com", year=2)
    brian = Student(name="Brian Obot", email="brianobot9@gmail.com", year=1000)
except ValidationError as err:
    print(f"Failed to register student because: {err}")
else:
    print(james)
    print(grace)
    print(brian)

In just a few lines, we leverage Pydantic to define validations, resulting in cleaner and more maintainable code. The validation error messages also provide immediate feedback, making debugging simpler.

Key Features of Pydantic

Type Annotation: The Power of Conventions

Pydantic’s expressive validation derives from Python’s type annotation system, allowing developers to explicitly define variable types. Here’s how type annotation works:

name: str = "Bruce Wayne"
age: int = 43
height_in_feets: float = 6.4

This flexibility enables you to define types without runtime enforcement. However, Pydantic utilizes annotations to enforce these checks when models are instantiated.

Common Type Annotations in Pydantic

  • str: Represents any string type, useful for names and addresses.
  • int: Represents whole numbers.
  • float: Represents floating-point numbers.
  • EmailStr: A specialized type to validate email formats right out of the box.

Data Coercion with Pydantic

Pydantic performs automatic data coercion, allowing types to be converted when possible to match defined schemas. This feature lessens the need for redundant conversion checks.

class Example(BaseModel):
    age: int

example = Example(age='25')
print(example.age)  # Output: 25

In this instance, Pydantic auto-converts the string '25' to the integer 25, enhancing code robustness and reducing potential user error.

Technical Deep-Dive Sections

Advanced Validation Techniques

Custom Validators

Pydantic supports validators that can enforce complex rules or conditions for model attributes. This offers control over how data is validated and transformed.

from pydantic import validator

class Student(BaseModel):
    name: str
    email: EmailStr
    year: int
    @validator('year')
    def validate_year(cls, value):
        if value < 1 or value > 6:
            raise ValueError('Year must be between 1 and 6')
        return value

The custom validator in the Student model ensures that the year is validated against the specified criteria.

Built-in and User-defined Validations

Utilizing built-in validators can tackle most common cases. However, when more complex rules are necessary, user-defined validation methods can introduce needed logic.

# User-defined validators for format and criteria
class User(BaseModel):
    username: str
    age: int

    @validator('username')
    def username_must_not_contain_spaces(cls, value):
        if ' ' in value:
            raise ValueError('Username must not contain spaces')
        return value

User-defined validators provide high customization based on specific app needs, thereby maintaining code clarity.

Serialization and Deserialization with Pydantic

Transforming Data Formats

Serialization allows Python objects to be transformed into formats such as JSON. Pydantic simplifies this process, allowing for straightforward conversion, ensuring that complex data types are adequately formatted.

student = Student(name="James Okon", email="james@mail.com", year=1)
student_json = student.json()
print(student_json)

This snippet serializes the Student instance into JSON for efficient transmission across web services or for storage.

Deserializing Data

Pydantic also parses JSON strings into Python objects, automatically inferring types and validating data upon model construction.

data = '{"name": "James Okon", "email": "james@mail.com", "year": 2}'
