student_instance = Student.parse_raw(data)
print(student_instance)

This example illustrates how incoming data can be efficiently parsed and validated, streamlining data intake processes.

Working with Nested Models

Creating Hierarchical Data Structures

Pydantic’s design allows for the representation of nested data structures through multiple models. This design is particularly useful in RESTful APIs where data returned often contains multiple layers.

from typing import List

class Course(BaseModel):
    title: str
    credits: int
class StudentWithCourses(BaseModel):
    name: str
    email: EmailStr
    courses: List[Course]

This model shows how Pydantic handles complex hierarchies and encapsulates related data naturally.

Handling Lists and Dicts

When collections like lists or dictionaries come into play, Pydantic validates and parses items effectively, facilitating robust data handling strategies.

class GroupedStudents(BaseModel):
    group_name: str
    students: List[Student]

group = GroupedStudents(group_name="Freshmen", students=[james, grace])
print(group.json())

Here, Pydantic allows seamless handling of multi-part data constructs, making it a powerful tool for managing related datasets.

Edge Cases with Pydantic

Handling Optional Fields

Often, datasets contain optional fields. Pydantic allows these fields to be declared using Optional and will validate their presence and data type correctly.

from typing import Optional

class StudentWithOptional(BaseModel):
    name: str
    email: EmailStr
    year: int
    phone: Optional[str] = None  # This field is optional


student = StudentWithOptional(name="Mary Jane", email="mary.jane@mail.com", year=2)
print(student.phone)  # Output: None because no phone number was provided

In this case, the phone field can either have a value or be absent, which Pydantic handles gracefully.

Complex Nested Validations

Pydantic models can also contain nested models, allowing for validations that span multiple levels of data structures.

class Teacher(BaseModel):
    name: str
    email: EmailStr

class School(BaseModel):
    name: str
    teachers: List[Teacher]
school_data = {
    "name": "Springfield High",
    "teachers": [
        {"name": "Mr. Smith", "email": "smith@school.com"},
        {"name": "Ms. Johnson", "email": "johnson@school.com"},
    ]
}
school = School(**school_data)
print(school.json())

This snippet demonstrates how complex data structures can be validated all at once, thanks to Pydantic’s capabilities.

Real-World Applications of Pydantic

In practical deployment, Pydantic’s utility shines. Many web applications and APIs leverage Pydantic for data validation and serialization, contributing immensely to reliability and clarity of data handling.

Applications in FastAPI

One of the most compelling showcases of Pydantic’s capabilities arises in the context of FastAPI, a modern web framework that utilizes Pydantic heavily for request validation and response serialization.

Example FastAPI integration with Pydantic is illustrated below:

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()
class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    description: str = None
    price: float
    tax: float = None
@app.post("/items/")
async def create_item(item: Item):
    return item

In this FastAPI app, Pydantic is instrumental in defining and enforcing expected input formats for the endpoint /items/, facilitating straightforward integration and error management.

Applications in Machine Learning

Data validation and processing pipelines in machine learning applications are crucial for managing incoming data. Pydantic ensures that datasets conform to expected formats and types, simplifying preprocessing and reducing errors in training models.

from pydantic import BaseModel

class UserProfile(BaseModel):
    name: str
    age: int
    email: EmailStr
    preferences: List[str] = []
# Processing dimensionality reduction
def validate_user_data(user_data: dict) -> UserProfile:
    return UserProfile(**user_data)

In this snippet, incoming user profiles are validated to ensure the data integrity required for further processing steps, improving model reliability.

Conclusion

In conclusion, Pydantic emerges as an extremely efficient tool for validating data in Python applications. By mastering its core features—including type annotations, built-in serialization, custom validations, and handling complex data structures—Python developers can significantly improve their data validation strategies. Pydantic’s versatility paves the way for easily creating scalable and maintainable codebases that uphold high standards of data integrity.

As you continue your journey with Pydantic, consider how its features can be applied to enhance the functionality and reliability of your applications. Mastering Pydantic not only enriches your skill set but also positions you favorably for tackling complex challenges in Python software development.

For more expansive insights and practical examples, refer to the Pydantic documentation.

entry.title: I Finally Understand References and Lifetimes in Rust
entry.content:
Introduction

I have been learning and working with Rust for over a year now, and for most of that time, I felt as if I understood references and how to use them. However, for lifetimes, I made a conscious effort not to get my life entangled with that concept. It wasn’t until recently that I gained a new perspective on them that they finally made sense. Understanding these concepts has been pivotal not just in writing correct code, but also in grasping why Rust’s memory guarantees provide safety and performance.

Understanding References in Rust

References are pointers to a value or part of data; they don’t store the data themselves, just the pointer to where the data is stored in memory (they store the address of another item in memory). This distinction is crucial for understanding how to manage memory safely in Rust.

From the image above, val is a variable that holds the value 1. Taking a reference to that variable stores the address of val in another variable.

Validity of References

When you create a reference to a value, that reference should only be valid until that value is freed or changed. When the freeing of the value occurs, it is dropped from memory, and that memory address is no longer valid for that value. Consequently, that reference is also invalidated.

  • Attempting to use a reference after its associated value has been dropped leads to a compiler error.
  • Furthermore, if the value is changed, the memory address of that value can also change.

This is especially common for values stored on the Heap, where memory management is dynamic and subject to change. Rust’s compiler enforces these rules, ensuring that all references remain valid during their lifetime.

Lock-on Behavior of References

Valid references can be thought of as lock-on values that, when acquired, ensure that the underlying value is accessed only in read-only mode.

  • If you want to modify that value, the original reference must be mutable, enabling you to change the underlying data.
  • Moreover, if the memory address of the original value is changed—either due to reallocation or modification—the reference will become invalid. Accessing it afterwards will result in a compiler error.

This behavior reinforces Rust’s objectives of safe concurrency by preventing dangling references—references that point to a memory location that has already been freed.

Technical Deep-Dive: The Ownership Model in Rust

Key Concepts of Ownership

Rust employs an ownership model that is central to its design and memory safety guarantees.

  • Each Value has an Owner: Each value in Rust is associated with a variable that acts as its owner.
  • Single Ownership: There can only be one owner of a value at any given time. This guarantees that when the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped, thereby preventing memory leaks.

Ownership and Memory Management

This unique model fosters straightforward memory management without the need for a garbage collector. The compiler and ownership rules ensure that memory is reclaimed as soon as it is no longer needed, leading to high performance and zero overhead in most cases.

Example Code: Ownership and Scoping

fn main() {
    let string_value = String::from("hello");
    
    {
      let greetings = String::from("Hello there!"); // greetings is valid in this scop
    } // greetings is no longer valid once we exit this scope.

    let mut name = String::from("Brian");
    name.push_str(" David");
    println!("Name: {}", name);
}

In this example, greetings is a temporary variable that goes out of scope, thereby freeing its associated memory. Meanwhile, the name variable retains ownership of its data until it goes out of scope.

Technical Deep-Dive: References & Lifetimes

What are Lifetimes?

Lifetimes in Rust ensure that references are valid for as long as they need to be. Every reference in Rust has a lifetime, signifying the scope within which that reference is valid.

Rules of Lifetimes:

  • Each Reference has a Lifetime: This signifies how long the reference is valid in relation to the data it points to.
  • No Dangling References: The Rust compiler checks that all references remain valid at compile time, thus preventing any accidental use of dangling references.

Using Lifetimes in Function Signatures

When functions take references as parameters, it is crucial to indicate the relationship between the lifetimes of the input and output references using lifetime annotations.

Example Code: Function with Lifetime Annotations

fn longest<'a>(s1: &'a str, s2: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if s1.len() > s2.len() {
        s1
    } else {
        s2
    }
}

In this example, 'a indicates that both input references must live at least as long as the returned reference. These annotations allow the Rust compiler to enforce correct memory management rules.

Advanced Concepts: Lifetime Elision

Rust also employs lifetime elision, which simplifies writing functions by allowing the compiler to infer lifetimes based on specific patterns. This means you can often omit lifetime annotations in straightforward cases, allowing for cleaner and more concise code.

Example Code: Lifetime Elision in Practice

fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str {
    let bytes = s.as_bytes();
    for (i, &item) in bytes.iter().enumerate() {
        if item == b' ' {
            return &s[0..i]; // Return a slice of the string
        }
    }
    &s[..] // Return the entire string if no space was found
}

In the above code, the compiler can infer that the returned reference has the same lifetime as the input s, thereby avoiding the need for explicit annotations.

References and Lifetimes in Structs

Using references dynamically in structs can complicate things, especially when you want to ensure that the struct does not outlive the references it holds.

Example Code: Struct with Lifetimes

struct Book<'a> {
    title: &'a str,
    author: &'a str,
}

fn main() {
    let title = String::from("Rust Programming");
    let author = String::from("Jane Doe");
    let book = Book {
        title: &title,
        author: &author,
    };
    println!("Book Title: {}, Author: {}", book.title, book.author);
}

In this example, the Book struct contains references to title and author. The lifetimes specified through the struct ensure that these references live at least as long as the Book instance itself.

Borrowing Mutably vs. Immutably

In Rust, when you borrow a value, you can choose to do so immutably or mutably, and this choice has significant implications for lifetimes and references.

Example Code: Immutable and Mutable Borrowing

fn main() {
    let mut value = 10;

    let ref1 = &value; // Immutable borrow
    // let ref2 = &mut value; // Error: cannot borrow `value` as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable
    println!("Immutable Reference: {}", ref1);
    let ref2 = &mut value; // Mutable borrow after immutable borrow ends
    *ref2 += 5; // Modifying the value through mutable reference
    println!("Modified Value: {}", ref2);
}

In this case, you can see how immutably borrowing value prevents you from getting a mutable reference until the immutable reference goes out of scope.

Technical Deep-Dive: Common Pitfalls When Working with References and Lifetimes

Working with references and lifetimes can lead to some common issues, particularly for those new to Rust. It’s essential to be aware of these pitfalls to effectively manage memory and prevent compiler errors.

Dangling References

Creating a reference to a local variable can cause dangling references. When the local variable goes out of scope, the reference to that variable remains, leading to potential undefined behavior if accessed.

Example Code: Dangling Reference

fn create_dangling_reference() -> &String {
    let str = String::from("Dangling Reference");
    &str // Error: return of reference to local variable `str`
}

The above code will raise a compile-time error because str is dropped at the end of the function, leaving the returned reference dangling.

Lifetimes Mismatch

Another common issue arises when the lifetimes of references provided to a function do not match the expected lifetimes defined in function signatures. This can lead to confusion and compiler errors.

Example Code: Lifetime Mismatch

fn incorrect_lifetime<'a>(s1: &'a str, s2: &str) -> &'a str {
    if s1.len() > s2.len() {
        s1
    } else {
        s2 // Error: the returned reference may not outlive `s2`
    }
}

In this case, the function attempts to return a reference from s1, tied to a specific lifetime 'a, while s2 does not have that constraint.

Borrow Checker Confusion

Rust’s borrow checker enforces strict rules for borrowing, which can lead to misunderstandings for new programmers. Understanding when ownership transfers and when immutability or mutability can be used is critical.

Example Code: Borrow Checker Issues

fn main() {
    let mut number = 10;
    let reference1 = &number; // Immutable borrow
    let reference2 = &mut number; // Error: cannot borrow `number` as mutable due to previous immutable borrow
    println!("Number: {}", reference1);
}

The compiler will generate an error when trying to create a mutable reference while an immutable reference still exists.

Conclusion

Navigating through references and lifetimes in Rust can seem overwhelming at first. However, the language’s design promotes safety and concurrency without a garbage collector. Understanding the ownership model, the nature of references, and how lifetimes work paves the way for better coding practices in Rust.

By learning these concepts, my confidence in leveraging Rust’s memory guarantees has greatly improved. Rust encourages developers to think critically about memory usage, leading to highly efficient programs that are safe from unexpected behavior.

If you want deeper insights into Rust’s memory model, I recommend checking out the official Rust documentation and exploring the various use cases of references and lifetimes. For practical Rust examples, you can refer to the Rust Book for a comprehensive understanding and practical implementation.

The combination of references, lifetimes, and the ownership model forms the backbone of Rust’s memory safety and performance. While challenging at first, mastering these concepts leads to robust and efficient Rust code that stands the test of time, makes concurrent programming easier, and ultimately, enhances the developer experience.

entry.title: Mastering Python Performance: The Small Tweaks That Make Big Speed
entry.content:
Introduction

In the realm of software development, writing functional code is often just the beginning. The delicate balance between efficiency, execution duration, and code complexity can make or break your software, particularly in performance-critical applications. For instance, in algorithmic trading, microsecond differences can determine profitable entries. In this guide, you will acquire a comprehensive mental model for optimizing your Python code and learn how to extend this knowledge to enhance your applications’ overall performance.

TL;DR

If you are looking for quick pointers to boost your Python code efficiency, check out the key topics below or jump to specific sections:

  • Favor constants over variables
  • Utilize sets for efficient look-ups
  • Leverage built-in constructs for optimization
  • Explore memory management techniques
  • Understand algorithm complexity
  • Optimize I/O-bound operations
  • Employ multi-threading and parallel processing

Core Performance Principles

Favor Constants Over Variables

While variables may enhance code readability, every time a variable is accessed, the Python interpreter must load the value from memory. Constants, in contrast, can be accessed directly, which introduces a speed advantage.

import dis

def add_const():
    return 10 + 100

def add_var(a, b):
    return a + b


print("Bytecode for Add Const")
print(dis.dis(add_const))
print("Bytecode for Add Var")
print(dis.dis(add_var))

In this simplified example, even though the efficiency gains by using constants may seem trivial, understanding these nuances can significantly influence code structure. The key lies in systematically using constants where appropriate while ensuring readability is not compromised. Constants reduce the overhead associated with variable lookups, thereby contributing to more efficient execution times.

Use Sets for Lookups

When your code requires frequent membership tests (checking if a value exists in a collection), sets outpace lists and tuples significantly due to their underlying hash table implementation.

# Using a list for lookups
my_list = list(range(100000000000))
if 2000000 in my_list:
    print("Found!")

# Using a set for lookups
my_set = set(range(100000000000))
if 2000000in my_set:
    print("Found!")

Sets deliver O(1) average time complexity for look-up operations, making them the ideal choice for performance-critical applications. By using sets, you can avoid the linear time complexity associated with lists. This efficiency can make a substantial difference in applications where repeated lookups occur in a large dataset.

Leverage Built-In Constructs for Optimization

Another crucial aspect of writing efficient Python code involves leveraging built-in constructs that Python provides out of the box. Python’s standard libraries, including functools, itertools, and collections, contain optimized implementations that can enhance performance.

Using functools.lru_cache for Caching

One of the simplest yet highly effective optimizations involves caching results of function calls that are expensive to compute using lru_cache.

from functools import lru_cache

@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def fibonacci(n):
    if n < 2:
        return n
    return fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2)
print(fibonacci(30))  # Efficiently computed using caching

By applying caching, you avoid redundant computations, which can save considerable time, particularly in recursive algorithms.

Technical Deep-Dive Sections

Deep-Dive Section 1: Understanding Python’s Memory Management

Introduction to Memory Management

Python employs dynamic memory management through its object allocator. Understanding how Python handles memory allocation and garbage collection can equip you with strategies to write more efficient code. Memory management techniques are crucial for optimizing resource usage and minimizing lag.

The Role of the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL)

Python’s Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) prevents multiple native threads from executing Python bytecodes at once. This design choice simplifies memory management but can also restrict performance in CPU-bound programs. To circumvent this, consider concurrent or parallel processing techniques, such as using the multiprocessing module to create separate memory spaces.

Strategies for Efficient Memory Use

  • Use Generators: Instead of returning large data sets, use generators to yield items one at a time, conserving memory.
def count_down(n):     
    while n > 0:         
      yield n         
      n -= 1
  • Pool Resources: Utilize ThreadPoolExecutor or ProcessPoolExecutor from the concurrent.futures library to manage thread and process pools efficiently. This strategy can lead to improved responsiveness in your applications.
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor  


def task(n):     
    return n * n  

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=5) as executor:     
    results = executor.map(task, range(10))

These strategies aim to optimize memory access and allocation, reducing the overhead of data processing in Python applications.

Deep-Dive Section 2: Algorithm Complexity Analysis

Introduction to Big O Notation

Understanding how operations scale with data input sizes is crucial for optimizing performance. Big O notation provides a high-level understanding of an algorithm’s efficiency. This notation helps developers categorize algorithms based on their time complexity characteristics.

Analyzing Common Python Algorithms

Analyze the time and space complexity of common operations, explaining distinctions between lists, sets, and dictionaries. Consider the following:

  • Sorting Lists: O(n log n)
  • Searching through Sets/Dictionaries: O(1) average
  • Iterating through Lists: O(n)

Here is another practical example:

def find_duplicates(data):
    seen = set()
    duplicates = []
    for number in data:
        if number in seen:
            duplicates.append(number)
        seen.add(number)
    return duplicates

In this code, using a set for lookups maintains O(1) complexity for checking the existence of previously-seen numbers, showcasing the speed advantage of using appropriate data structures.

Practical Examples

Providing code snippets illustrating computational complexities in realistic scenarios solidifies understanding. Here’s an example of an efficient search function:

def binary_search(arr, target):
    low, high = 0, len(arr) - 1
    while low <= high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        if arr[mid] < target:
            low = mid + 1
        elif arr[mid] > target:
            high = mid - 1
        else:
            return mid
    return -1

The binary search algorithm operates in O(log n) time, making it significantly more efficient for large, sorted datasets compared to the linear search.

Deep-Dive Section 3: Optimizing I/O-Bound Operations

Exploring I/O-Bound Performance Challenges

In many applications, I/O operations (like reading and writing to disk, or network requests) can often become bottlenecks. When designing your software, consider asynchronous programming models that allow for overlapping I/O operations to enhance overall speed.

Employing Asyncio for Non-Blocking I/O

By utilizing the asyncio module, Python provides a way to manage I/O-bound operations more efficiently. This can prevent blocking during data retrieval or processing, which is crucial for applications that require responsiveness.

import asyncio

async def fetch_data():
    await asyncio.sleep(1)  # Simulate a network call
    return "data fetched!"
async def main():
    data = await fetch_data()
    print(data)
asyncio.run(main())

With asyncio, you can perform I/O operations without stalling other processes, which can considerably improve efficiency, especially in web applications and services.

Multi-threading and Parallel Processing

Benefits of Multi-threading

When dealing with I/O-bound tasks, consider applying multi-threading alongside asynchronous I/O. Python’s threading module allows for concurrent execution of code, which can improve responsiveness in applications that require simultaneous operations.

import threading

def worker():
    print("Worker thread is executing.")
threads = []

for i in range(5):
    thread = threading.Thread(target=worker)
    threads.append(thread)
    thread.start()
for thread in threads:
    thread.join()

By launching multiple threads, you can manage several tasks in parallel, thereby reducing the total execution time for operations such as web scraping or downloading multiple files.

Exploring Multi-processing

For CPU-bound tasks, consider using the multiprocessing module, which allows you to create processes that run in their own memory space. This approach can bypass the limitations imposed by the GIL and effectively utilize multiple CPU cores.

from multiprocessing import Process

def task(n):
    print(f'Process {n} is executing.')

processes = []
for i in range(5):
    process = Process(target=task, args=(i,))
    processes.append(process)
    process.start()
for process in processes:
    process.join()

The multi-processing module instantiates separate processes for each task, leveraging the full capabilities of your CPU. This technique is especially beneficial when you require intensive computations, such as numerical simulations or data processing.

Conclusion

In summary, while functionality is paramount, considering performance in your code design is essential for ensuring efficient execution in any application. By leveraging constants, optimizing data structures, understanding algorithm complexity, and employing techniques for asynchronous and parallel processing, you can refine your codebase for better performance.

The strategies covered herein offer foundational principles that you can apply across various projects, contributing to a culture of performance-driven development. Continue to learn and adapt these methodologies as you advance in your Python journey to create more efficient and robust applications.

The importance of writing performant code cannot be overstressed in modern software development. By implementing small but impactful tweaks, you can drastically improve the speed and efficiency of your Python applications. Continue to explore threading, asynchronous I/O, and memory management concepts to enhance your skills further. Sharing your discoveries with your peers can foster collaboration and collective growth in programming quality.

Should you find additional optimizations, document your findings, and do not hesitate to contribute back to the Python community. Happy coding!

entry.title: Mastering the Crate and Module System in Rust
entry.content:
Introduction

Once your program or project starts to grow, the need to introduce more files and organize your project's structure becomes crucial to maintaining sanity and ensuring a productive coding environment. Rust offers the concepts of crates and modules, and mastering these can help you shape your next project in a systematic way that enhances understanding and contributions to larger Rust projects. This piece will dive into the intricacies of the crate and module system, providing clarity on their roles, differences, and the best practices around them.

Packages are not Crates, and Vice Versa

This has often been the stumbling block for many developers new to Rust. Common materials assert that crates are the building blocks of Rust projects and, by extension, the smallest unit of compilation. This leads to the misconception that when a new project is created, that project is, in itself, a crate. However, this is not true.

Creating a New Project

When you start a new project using Cargo with the command:

$ cargo new rust-projects

The output indicates that a binary application package has been created:

Created binary (application) `rust-projects` package

This initializes your project directory and generates several files. The hierarchical structure of the generated files appears as follows:

$ ls rust-projects
Cargo.toml
src

$ ls rust-projects/src
main.rs

Every package contains a Cargo.toml file and a src directory with a main.rs file (in the binary case), but the package itself is not the crate. It is technically correct to refer to a package in Rust as a folder containing a Cargo.toml file — you can make a regular directory a package by adding a valid Cargo.toml file.

Crates Explained

When a package is created, Rust automatically generates a binary crate rooted at src/main.rs. If you wish to create a library crate, you can use:

$ cargo new --lib <lib-package-name>

This generates a standard Cargo package, but houses a lib.rs file instead of main.rs. The distinction between files like main.rs and lib.rs is crucial, as it indicates whether a package is a binary or a library.

Key Definitions

  • Package: A housing unit for crates. A package contains at least one crate rooted at src/main.rs or src/lib.rs.
  • Crate: The compiled piece of code, which can either be a binary or a library. Each package allows for multiple binary crates (and can also include dependencies).

By defining packages and crates in this way, it becomes easier to grasp syntax such as crate::<path>. This directly translates to the <path> item located in the src/main.rs file, which is the crate root for binary packages, and src/lib.rs for library packages.

Modules: The Organizational Structure

While packages help you group crates at a project level, modules provide a structured organization for different features or parts of your code. Think of your package as a house filled with various items sourced from various brands — some you create and others you buy. It's your responsibility to organize these items in a way that makes sense for your desired house setting.

The Importance of Modules

Consider a house where all items are crammed together. This leads to confusion and makes it difficult to find the necessary items. The clearer the organization within your project or code, the more efficient you can be. This concept of organization is the primary benefit modules provide — not just in Rust, but in every programming language.

Basic Usage of Modules

To define a module in Rust, the mod keyword is utilized. For instance:

// src/main.rs

mod kitchen {
    struct Cooker(String);
    struct Heater(String);
    struct Table;
}

fn main() {
    println!("Hello World!");
}

Here, a module named kitchen is created, containing three structs: Cooker, Heater, and Table. To utilize an item from this module, the path to the item must be specified at the point where the item is needed.

Path to Items Inside Modules

If you need to access an item from this module:

// inside the main function
let cooker = kitchen::Cooker("Pressure Cooker".to_string());

This statement effectively directs Rust to navigate to the kitchen module to access the Cooker item.

Visibility in Modules

Items within modules are private by default, which means they are not accessible from outside unless designated as public using the pub keyword. For example:

mod kitchen {
    pub struct Cooker(String); // the String item inside the Cooker is private
    pub struct Heater(String); // so is the String item inside the Heater

    struct Table; // Still private
}

Even if Cooker is public, its contents remain private unless stated explicitly. This ensures encapsulation and keeps the module organized and maintainable.

Large Codebase Management in Rust

For projects evolving into larger codebases, managing dependencies and organization becomes critical. This section covers best practices for structuring large Rust projects.

Dependency Management

Cargo.toml: This central configuration file plays a crucial role in managing dependencies. You must specify the dependencies your crate is using here, enabling straightforward integration and updates. By allowing version control directly within this file, Rust ensures compatibility with the modules or packages you rely on.

[dependencies]
rand = "0.8"
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }

Using external crates: You can include external libraries available from crates.io, effectively reducing development time and enhancing functional capabilities.

# Adding an external crate
[dependencies]
log = "0.4"

Your project can then use external libraries seamlessly in your codebase, allowing for rich functionality with little overhead.

Module Organization Strategies

Logical grouping: Organizing functionality into logically cohesive modules reduces complexity. For instance, if you have functionality related to user management, implement that in a user.rs module, while maintaining a separate product.rs for product-related functionality. This keeps separation of concerns clear.

Namespacing: The use of prefixes in module names can help maintain clarity, especially when dealing with numerous modules. By structuring your modules distinctly, you can easily avoid naming collisions that would lead to conflicts at compile time.

Advanced Module Usage

Modules in Rust offer a breadth of functionality that can enhance code clarity and reusability. This section dives into advanced techniques for modules.

Nested Modules

Nested modules allow you to create more complex hierarchical structures, which can help in organizing similar functionality together. Here's an example of how to define nested modules:

mod server {
    pub mod routes {
        pub fn get_user() {
            println!("Getting user");
        }
    }

    pub mod handlers {
        pub fn handle_request() {
            println!("Handling request");
        }
    }
}

To access these nested modules, the syntax becomes a bit more complex. You need to specify the full path:

fn main() {
    server::routes::get_user();
    server::handlers::handle_request();
}

This organization not only keeps your project tidy but also clearly delineates functionality, making it easier for others to understand the codebase.

Public Interfaces and Privacy

Understanding visibility is crucial for maintaining a clean boundary between different parts of your code. Any item marked as pub can be accessed from the outside, while those without this modifier are private. Here's how to correctly declare visibility:

mod kitchen {
    pub struct Cooker(pub String); // Both the struct and its field are public.
    pub struct Heater(String); // Struct is public, but field remains private.

    impl Heater {
        // This method can be public if needed
        pub fn new(name: String) -> Heater {
            Heater(name)
        }
    }
}

This approach allows for a flexible API while maintaining internal encapsulation where necessary.

Performance Optimization with Modules

Understanding how to structure your modules and leverage Rust's compilation process can lead to optimized performance.

Optimizing for Compilation

When you split your code into smaller modules, Rust's incremental compilation can speed up the build process. When only one module is changed, only that particular module needs to be recompiled instead of the entire project. This can be a significant advantage in large applications.

Memory Usage

Using modules wisely can allow Rust to optimize memory usage at runtime. By compartmentalizing functionality, unnecessary data can often be discarded if it's only used within a particular context:

#[inline(always)]
fn expensive_function() -> Result<String, String> {
    // Hypothetical expensive operation
    Ok("Result".to_string())
}

By marking functions inline, you can reduce the overhead of function calls and streamline performance in high-frequency usage scenarios.

Working with Crates: Dependency Management and Structuring

Understanding how to manage and structure crates within Rust applications is key to building robust applications.

Cargo.toml: The Heartbeat of Dependency Management

The Cargo.toml file is crucial for managing dependencies and specifying package metadata. Here is how you can structure it:

[package]
name = "my_project"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2018"

[dependencies]
serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] }
chrono = "0.4"

By keeping dependencies well-organized and up to date, you ensure your project remains stable and compatible with other libraries.

Case Study: Real-world Application Structure

Consider a Rust web application structured for a blog. The project can be divided into several parts: a main entry point for the server, one for handling database interactions, one for authentication, and another for utility functions.

my_blog/
├── Cargo.toml
└── src/
    ├── main.rs   # Main entry point.
    ├── db.rs     # Database interactions.
    ├── auth.rs   # Authentication logic.
    └── utils.rs  # Utility functions.

Each module can be further divided upon reaching significant complexity, forming yet another layer of hierarchy.

Practical Examples and Use Cases

To solidify understanding, let's run through practical examples that demonstrate these concepts in action.

1. Basic Module Usage

Imagine a library to handle mathematical operations:

// src/math.rs

pub mod operations {
    pub fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 {
        a + b
    }

    pub fn multiply(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 {
        a * b
    }
}

You can call it directly within your main program:

// src/main.rs

mod math;

fn main() {
    let sum = math::operations::add(5, 7);
    let product = math::operations::multiply(5, 7);
    println!("Sum: {}, Product: {}", sum, product);
}

2. Using External Crates

Let's include the popular serde crate for serialization and deserialization. Here's how to use it:

# Cargo.toml

[dependencies]
serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1.0"
// src/user.rs

use serde::{Serialize, Deserialize};

#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct User {
    pub username: String,
    pub email: String,
}
// src/main.rs

mod user;

use user::User;

fn main() {
    let user = User {
        username: String::from("john_doe"),
        email: String::from("john.doe@example.com"),
    };

    let serialized_user = serde_json::to_string(&user).unwrap();
    println!("Serialized User: {}", serialized_user);
}

In this example, we're leveraging an external crate to efficiently handle data in our application.

Conclusion

Mastering the crate and module system in Rust is essential for building maintainable, scalable applications. Understanding the differences between packages and crates, along with the organizational capabilities offered by modules, allows you to create more efficient and effective codebases. By adopting the best practices highlighted throughout this article, you can elevate your programming skills and foster clean code structures that accommodate growth and complexity. Embrace these tools and watch your Rust projects flourish, ready to tackle broader functionality and larger codebases.

Technical Verdict

In conclusion, a profound understanding of crates and modules not only enhances your capability to write efficient Rust code but also empowers you to navigate complex projects confidently. With careful management of packages, robust dependency handling, and organized module structures, Rust developers can cultivate a prolific development environment conducive to both individual and collaborative growth.

By continuously expanding your knowledge and adapting your practices to leverage the power of crates and modules, you prepare yourself to create the next generation of Rust applications efficiently.

entry.title: The Double-Slit Experiment: How One Particle Interferes With Itself
entry.content:
Introduction

Richard Feynman once said the double-slit experiment contains "the only mystery" of quantum mechanics. Everything else that's weird about the quantum world, he argued, is some version of what happens here.

2025 was the International Year of Quantum Science and Technology, marking a hundred years since Heisenberg's 1925 paper that founded quantum mechanics. I spent part of it going back to the basics I had skimmed through in university physics, and the double-slit experiment was the one that kept pulling me back. It's simple enough to describe in a paragraph, and nobody has fully made peace with it in a century.

This post walks through it in three acts: with light, with particles, and with a detector watching. No maths beyond a couple of ratios, plus a short Python simulation you can run yourself.

TL;DR

  • Light through two narrow slits makes a pattern of bright and dark stripes (fringes). That's interference, the signature of a wave.
  • Send electrons through, one at a time, and each lands as a single dot. But the dots gradually build up the same striped pattern. Each electron seems to interfere with itself.
  • Put a detector at the slits to find out which slit each electron used, and the stripes vanish. You get two plain bands, as if they were bullets.
  • Quantum mechanics describes this with a wavefunction that passes through both slits, and the Born rule: the wave tells you only the probability of where a particle will be found.

Act one: light is a wave

In the early 1800s, Thomas Young shone light through two narrow, closely spaced slits onto a screen. If light were a stream of tiny particles, as Newton had argued, you'd expect two bright bands, one behind each slit. Instead Young saw a row of bright and dark stripes.

The explanation is interference, the same thing you see when two ripples cross on a pond. Light spreads out from each slit as a wave. At some points on the screen, the waves from the two slits arrive in step, crest on crest, and add up to a bright fringe. At others they arrive exactly out of step, crest on trough, and cancel to darkness.

Whether they arrive in step depends on the difference in distance from each slit. That gives a neat formula for the spacing between bright fringes:

fringe spacing = wavelength × screen distance / slit separation

Green light (500 nm) through slits 50 µm apart onto a screen 1 metre away gives fringes 1 cm apart. That's how 19th-century physicists measured the wavelength of light with nothing more than a ruler.

The crucial point: darkness appears in places that would be lit if only one slit were open. Open a second slit, and some spots on the screen get less light. Particles can't do that. Waves can.

So by about 1850 the question was settled: light is a wave. Then Einstein unsettled it in 1905 by showing light also arrives in discrete lumps of energy, photons. And in 1924, Louis de Broglie proposed the reverse: if waves can act like particles, maybe particles act like waves, with a wavelength set by their momentum:

λ = h / p

where h is Planck's constant. For anything you can see, that wavelength is absurdly small. For an electron, it's comparable to the spacing between atoms, which is why electron microscopes can see things light microscopes can't.

Act two: one electron at a time

Now the strange part. Replace the light with a beam of electrons, and turn the beam down so low that only one electron is in the apparatus at any moment. The screen is a detector that records exactly where each electron lands.

The famous version of this was done by Akira Tonomura's team at Hitachi in 1989, using an electron biprism (a fine charged wire that does the same job as two slits). Here's what they saw:

  1. Each electron arrives as a single dot, at a single point. Not smeared out. Not half here, half there. Particle-like.
  2. The positions look random. You can't predict where the next one will land.
  3. As thousands of dots accumulate, stripes appear. The same interference pattern as with light.

You can watch this happen with a short simulation. Each particle lands randomly, but the chance of landing at each point follows the brightness of the two-slit pattern:

import math
import random

WAVELENGTH = 500e-9   # metres (green light)
SLIT_GAP = 50e-6      # distance between the slits, metres
SCREEN = 1.0          # distance from slits to screen, metres
WIDTH = 0.03          # half-width of the screen we look at, metres

def intensity(y: float) -> float:
    """Relative brightness of the two-slit pattern at height y on the screen."""
    phase = math.pi * SLIT_GAP * y / (WAVELENGTH * SCREEN)
    return math.cos(phase) ** 2

def detect_one_particle() -> float:
    """Pick where a single particle lands, with probability set by intensity."""
    while True:
        y = random.uniform(-WIDTH, WIDTH)
        if random.random() < intensity(y):
            return y

def show(hits: int, bins: int = 60) -> None:
    counts = [0] * bins
    for _ in range(hits):
        y = detect_one_particle()
        counts[min(int((y + WIDTH) / (2 * WIDTH) * bins), bins - 1)] += 1
    peak = max(counts)
    shades = " .:-=+*#%@"
    row = "".join(shades[round(c / peak * (len(shades) - 1))] for c in counts)
    print(f"{hits:>6} particles |{row}|")

random.seed(1)
for n in (10, 100, 1_000, 10_000, 100_000):
    show(n)
    10 particles | @   =           =           =         =     =    @   =     |
   100 particles | **   ---%* : :  :**@--:    :-@- :    =-%=:    =-*--=-  :-**|
  1000 particles |#==.  .-%#*=-:  --*##==.  .:=*%*+.  .++*%+=.   -+#@+=:.. -#%|
 10000 particles |%*=:  :=#@%#=:  :=##%*+:  :=*@%#=:  :=*@%#=:  :=*@%*=:  :=#@|
100000 particles |@#=:  :=#@@#+:  :=#@@#+:  :=#@@#+:  :=#@@#=:  :=#@@#+:  :+#@|

At ten particles it's noise. By ten thousand, the fringes are unmistakable. (To be clear, this script assumes the interference pattern; it shows what the build-up looks like, not why it happens. The real experiment is the evidence.)

Now sit with what this means. There is only one electron in the apparatus at a time. There's no other electron for it to interfere with. Yet the dark fringes are places where electrons almost never land, places they would land if only one slit were open. Somehow, each individual electron is affected by both slits.

This isn't special to electrons. It's been done with neutrons, atoms, and in 1999 with buckyballs, football-shaped molecules of 60 carbon atoms. Anton Zeilinger's and Markus Arndt's groups in Vienna have since pushed it to molecules made of around 2,000 atoms. Everything interferes, if you can keep it isolated enough.

Act three: what if we look?

The natural instinct is to catch the electron in the act. Put a detector at the slits that registers which slit each electron passes through, and then see where it lands.

When you do this, the detector always reports one slit or the other, never both. And the interference pattern on the screen disappears. You get two overlapping bands, exactly what you'd expect from particles that each went through one slit.

Remove the detector, and the stripes come back.

It's tempting to say "the electron knows it's being watched", but that framing is misleading. There's nothing mystical about a conscious observer here. Any physical interaction that leaves a record of which slit was used, even a single stray photon bouncing off the electron that nobody ever looks at, destroys the interference. What matters is whether the information exists in the universe, not whether a person reads it.

Physicists call this complementarity (Niels Bohr's term): the setup can reveal wave-like behaviour (interference) or particle-like behaviour (which path), but not both fully at once. There's even a smooth trade-off. A weak detector that only partly tells you the path leaves you with faded fringes, and the better the path information, the fainter the stripes.

How quantum mechanics describes it

Quantum mechanics doesn't say the electron is "really" a wave or "really" a particle. It says the electron is described by a wavefunction, usually written ψ (psi). The wavefunction behaves exactly like a wave: it spreads out, goes through both slits, and interferes with itself.

But you never see the wavefunction directly. When the electron hits the screen, it's detected at a single point. Where it appears is random, and the Born rule, proposed by Max Born in 1926, gives the odds:

probability of finding the particle at a point ∝ |ψ|²

The wave decides the probabilities; each detection is a single event drawn from them. That's precisely what the simulation above does.

The interference lives in the wavefunction. With both slits open, ψ is the sum of a piece from each slit, ψ₁ + ψ₂, and squaring a sum gives cross terms that can be positive or negative. That's where the bright and dark fringes come from. When a detector records which slit was used, the two pieces become tied to different detector states, they can no longer interfere, and you're left with |ψ₁|² + |ψ₂|²: two plain bands.

So what is actually going on?

Here's where honest physicists stop agreeing. The maths is not in dispute; it predicts every result perfectly. What's disputed is what the maths means. A few of the main camps:

  • Copenhagen: the wavefunction is a tool for predicting measurement results. Asking which slit the electron "really" went through, when nothing recorded it, is not a meaningful question.
  • Pilot wave (de Broglie–Bohm): there really is a particle, always at a definite position, and it goes through one slit. But it's guided by a real wave that goes through both, and the wave steers it into the fringe pattern.
  • Many worlds: the wavefunction is all there is, and it never collapses. When a detector records the path, the universe branches into one where it went left and one where it went right.

All three predict the same experimental results, which is why the debate has lasted a century. I don't have a favourite yet. What I've come to appreciate is that each one makes you give up some piece of everyday intuition. You don't get to keep all of it.

Conclusion

The double-slit experiment is short to describe and impossible to un-learn:

  • Waves interfere, and dark fringes appear where a second open slit removes light.
  • Single particles build up interference patterns, one random dot at a time, as if each passes through both slits.
  • Recording the path destroys the pattern, whether or not anyone looks at the record.
  • Quantum mechanics captures it all with a wavefunction that interferes and the Born rule that turns it into probabilities. What that wavefunction is remains an open question.

If the double-slit experiment shows that quantum objects don't have a definite path, the next natural question is whether they have definite properties at all. That's where Heisenberg's uncertainty principle comes in.

entry.title: Nuclear Fission: How Splitting an Atom Powers a City
entry.content:
Introduction

In my previous post on binding energy I described nuclear energy as climbing a hill: nuclei release energy whenever they move towards iron, the most tightly bound nucleus there is. Light nuclei climb by fusing. Heavy nuclei climb by splitting.

This post is about the second route, fission, and it's the one humanity actually has working at scale. Roughly a tenth of the world's electricity comes from it today. As someone who studied electrical engineering, I spent years treating power stations as boxes that turn "heat" into electricity, without asking much about where the heat came from. In a nuclear plant, it comes from splitting atoms, and the physics of how that's done safely is more interesting than I expected.

You don't need to have read the previous post, but if terms like "binding energy per nucleon" are new to you, it's a quick detour.

TL;DR

  • A slow neutron hitting uranium-235 makes it wobble apart into two medium-sized nuclei, a few free neutrons, and about 200 MeV of energy.
  • Those freed neutrons can split more uranium, giving a chain reaction. The key number is the multiplication factor k: on average, how many new fissions each fission causes.
  • Bombs need k well above 1 and fast. Reactors need k held at exactly 1.
  • That's only possible because a small fraction of neutrons arrive seconds late. These delayed neutrons slow the reactor's response enough for control rods to keep up.

A short history

Fission was discovered almost by accident. In December 1938, Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann in Berlin were bombarding uranium with neutrons, expecting to make slightly heavier elements. Instead, their careful chemistry kept turning up barium, an element barely half uranium's mass.

Hahn wrote to his long-time collaborator Lise Meitner, who had fled Nazi Germany to Sweden. Over the Christmas holiday, Meitner and her nephew Otto Frisch worked out what was happening: the uranium nucleus wasn't being chipped, it was splitting in two. They estimated the energy released at around 200 MeV per split, borrowed the word "fission" from biology, and published in early 1939.

Within four years, on 2 December 1942, Enrico Fermi's team in Chicago ran the first self-sustaining chain reaction in a pile of graphite and uranium under a stadium. Nature had beaten them to it, though: around two billion years ago, uranium deposits at Oklo in Gabon ran as natural fission reactors, on and off, for hundreds of thousands of years. Groundwater acted as the moderator.

How a nucleus splits

The liquid drop picture

A heavy nucleus like uranium is held together by the short-range strong force and pushed apart by the repulsion between its 92 protons. It's like a drop of liquid with surface tension barely holding against a charge trying to blow it apart.

When uranium-235 absorbs a neutron, it becomes uranium-236 in an excited state, carrying an extra ~6.5 MeV of energy. That energy sets the drop oscillating. It stretches into a peanut shape, and once the neck between the two lobes gets thin enough, the electric repulsion between the lobes wins over the strong force across the neck. The drop snaps.

The energy needed to reach that snapping point is the fission barrier, about 6 MeV for uranium-236. The neutron's arrival delivers more than that, so fission happens readily.

Why U-235 and not U-238

Natural uranium is 99.3% uranium-238 and only 0.7% uranium-235. Why does everyone care about the rare one?

It comes down to pairing. Nucleons like to be in pairs. U-235 has an odd number of neutrons (143), so when it captures one, the new neutron completes a pair and the nucleus gets a bonus chunk of binding energy, enough to clear the fission barrier even if the incoming neutron was moving slowly.

U-238 already has an even number of neutrons (146). Adding one more leaves an unpaired neutron, so the energy bonus is smaller and falls short of the barrier. U-238 only fissions if the neutron brings in more than about 1 MeV of kinetic energy of its own.

Nuclei that fission with slow neutrons are called fissile: U-235, U-233 and plutonium-239 are the important ones. This is why reactor fuel is enriched: commercial reactors typically use uranium that's 3–5% U-235.

A typical split

There's no single way for U-236 to break. It splits asymmetrically, usually into one fragment around mass 95 and another around mass 140. One common example:

²³⁵U + n  →  ²³⁶U*  →  ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3n

Check the bookkeeping: mass numbers 235 + 1 = 141 + 92 + 3 = 236, and protons 92 = 56 + 36. Nothing is created or destroyed, just rearranged.

Where the 200 MeV goes

Barium and krypton both sit closer to iron on the binding energy curve than uranium does. Each nucleon gains just under 1 MeV of binding, and with ~236 nucleons that sums to around 200 MeV.

I can estimate it with the semi-empirical mass formula from the previous post, by comparing the binding energy of the products to the binding energy of the compound nucleus:

released = binding_energy(56, 141) + binding_energy(36, 92) - binding_energy(92, 236)
print(f"U-236 -> Ba-141 + Kr-92 + 3n releases about {released:.0f} MeV")
# U-236 -> Ba-141 + Kr-92 + 3n releases about 155 MeV

A rough formula gives 155 MeV for the split itself, a bit below the measured ~170 MeV for this channel, but the right ballpark. The rest comes later: the fragments are packed with too many neutrons and beta-decay over the following seconds to years, releasing more energy as they go.

Averaged over all fissions, the budget for U-235 looks roughly like this:

Where the energy goesMeV
Kinetic energy of the two fragments~169
Kinetic energy of the free neutrons~5
Prompt gamma rays~7
Beta and gamma decay of fragments~13
Antineutrinos (escape, lost)~10
Total~200

The bulk of it is the two fragments flying apart, pushed by their mutual electric repulsion. They slam into surrounding atoms within a few micrometres and their kinetic energy becomes heat. That's the heat that boils water and spins turbines.

Note the fragment decay line. That energy keeps coming even after the chain reaction stops. Right after shutdown, a reactor still produces about 6–7% of its full power as decay heat, falling to around 1% after a few hours. This is why reactors need cooling long after they're switched off, and why losing that cooling at Fukushima in 2011 was a disaster even though the reactors had already shut down.

Putting it in perspective

200 MeV per atom is about 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ joules, which sounds tiny. But a kilogram of U-235 has around 2.6 × 10²⁴ atoms, so fissioning all of it releases about 82 terajoules. A kilogram of good coal gives about 25 megajoules. That's a ratio of over three million to one.

The chain reaction

Each fission releases on average about 2.4 neutrons. If at least one of those goes on to cause another fission, the process sustains itself. The number that matters is the multiplication factor:

k = (fissions in this generation) / (fissions in the previous generation)
  • k < 1, subcritical: the reaction dies out.
  • k = 1, critical: the reaction holds steady. This is a reactor running normally.
  • k > 1, supercritical: the reaction grows exponentially.

Note that "critical" is a calm, steady state, not an emergency, despite how films use the word.

Not every neutron causes another fission. Some escape through the surface. Some get absorbed by U-238, structural materials, or fission products without causing a split. So k depends on the material, its enrichment, its shape, and its size. That last one leads to the idea of critical mass: a lump has to be big enough that neutrons are more likely to hit another nucleus than leak out. For a bare sphere of pure U-235 that's around 50 kg; for plutonium-239 it's around 10 kg.

Slowing neutrons down: the moderator

Neutrons are born fast, at around 2 MeV. But U-235 is hundreds of times more likely to absorb a slow (thermal) neutron than a fast one. So most reactors deliberately slow their neutrons down with a moderator.

The trick is to let the neutrons bounce off light nuclei. Think of snooker: a ball hitting another ball of the same mass can lose all its speed in one collision, but a ball hitting a bowling ball just bounces off at almost the same speed. Hydrogen, with nearly the same mass as a neutron, is the best at this. That's why ordinary water is the moderator (and coolant) in most reactors in the world. Graphite and heavy water are the common alternatives, both absorbing fewer neutrons, which is why reactors moderated with them can run on unenriched natural uranium.

Water moderation also gives a built-in safety feature: if the water overheats and turns to steam, it gets less dense, moderates less, and k drops. The reactor turns itself down.

Why reactors can be controlled at all

This is the part that genuinely surprised me when I first worked through the numbers.

In a water-moderated reactor, a neutron generation lasts somewhere around 0.1 milliseconds: born, slowed down, absorbed, causing the next fission. That's 10,000 generations per second. If k were even slightly above 1, say 1.001, the power would multiply by 1.001^10000, about 22,000 times, in a single second. No mechanical control rod could possibly keep up.

The rescue is that not all neutrons arrive instantly. About 0.65% of the neutrons from U-235 fission are delayed: they're emitted by fission fragments that decay a few seconds to a minute later. The average delay is around 13 seconds.

0.65% sounds negligible, but it stretches the average time between generations dramatically. Here's the arithmetic:

import math

PROMPT_LIFETIME = 1e-4    # seconds between neutron generations, prompt only
BETA = 0.0065             # fraction of U-235 fission neutrons that are delayed
DELAY = 12.7              # mean delay of those neutrons, in seconds

def growth_after(seconds: float, k: float, lifetime: float) -> float:
    """Factor the neutron population (and power) grows by after `seconds`."""
    period = lifetime / (k - 1)
    return math.exp(seconds / period)

effective_lifetime = PROMPT_LIFETIME + BETA * DELAY

for k in (1.0001, 1.001):
    prompt = growth_after(1.0, k, PROMPT_LIFETIME)
    delayed = growth_after(1.0, k, effective_lifetime)
    print(f"k = {k}: prompt only x{prompt:,.1f} per second, with delayed neutrons x{delayed:.3f} per second")
k = 1.0001: prompt only x2.7 per second, with delayed neutrons x1.001 per second
k = 1.001: prompt only x22,026.5 per second, with delayed neutrons x1.012 per second

With delayed neutrons included, the effective generation time is closer to 0.08 seconds, and the same slight excess in k grows the power by about 1% per second instead of 22,000-fold. That's slow enough for control rods, made of neutron-hungry materials like boron or cadmium, to be moved in and out to keep k at exactly 1.

The golden rule of reactor design follows from this: the reactor must never be critical on prompt neutrons alone. As long as it needs the delayed neutrons to stay critical, it changes slowly enough to control. Chernobyl in 1986 is the tragic counterexample: a combination of design flaws and operating decisions pushed reactor 4 past this line, and its power spiked by orders of magnitude in seconds.

A bomb is the opposite. It has no moderator, no delayed neutrons to wait for, and it's assembled to be strongly supercritical on fast neutrons. The whole reaction is over in about a microsecond.

Inside a power reactor

Putting the pieces together, a typical pressurised water reactor looks like this:

  1. Fuel: pellets of uranium dioxide enriched to 3–5% U-235, stacked in long metal rods, bundled into assemblies.
  2. Moderator and coolant: water flows between the rods, slowing neutrons and carrying heat away. It's held at about 155 bar so it stays liquid at around 300 °C.
  3. Control rods: slide between fuel rods to absorb neutrons and adjust k. Dissolved boron in the water provides fine adjustment.
  4. Steam generator: the hot, pressurised water heats a separate water loop, which boils.
  5. Turbine and generator: the steam spins a turbine connected to a generator. From here on it's the same as a coal or gas plant.

That last step is the humbling part for an electrical engineer: all that nuclear physics, and at the end of the day it's an extremely sophisticated kettle.

The catch: waste

The fission fragments that made the energy are themselves the problem. They're neutron-rich and intensely radioactive. Some, like caesium-137 and strontium-90, have half-lives around 30 years. On top of that, U-238 in the fuel absorbs neutrons and turns into plutonium and other heavy elements, some of which stay radioactive for tens of thousands of years.

The volume is small. All the spent fuel a large reactor produces in a year would fit in a modest room. But it has to be cooled for years, then isolated for millennia. Finland's Onkalo repository, carved into bedrock hundreds of metres down, is the first deep geological disposal site for spent fuel. For most countries, though, the long-term plan is still a plan.

Conclusion

Fission is the side of the binding energy hill we have actually conquered. The core ideas:

  • U-235 splits easily because absorbing one neutron completes a pair and pushes it over the fission barrier.
  • ~200 MeV per fission, mostly the kinetic energy of two fragments repelling each other, which becomes heat.
  • Chain reactions are governed by k, and reactors live at k = 1.
  • Delayed neutrons are the quiet hero: a 0.65% sliver of late neutrons is the difference between a power station and an uncontrollable spike.

Fission's drawbacks, long-lived waste, the risk of losing cooling, and its link to weapons, are exactly what make the other side of the hill so tempting. In the next post I'll look at fusion: what it would take to build a star on Earth, and why it's taken so long.

entry.title: Setting Up Rust Analyzer to work for Non-Cargo-Based Rust Projects
entry.content:
Introduction

While working on the Advent of Code Challenge for this year, I planned to solve the challenges in Python and the Rust Programming Language, and after solving the first 2 days in Python, I decided to solve those in Rust too, it didn’t take long before I realized how difficult I found it working with Rust programs without the benefits of a Language server like Rust Analyzer.

The Problem

Rust Analyzer is built around Cargo. When you run:

cargo new my_project

Cargo quietly generates the metadata Rust Analyzer relies on to understand your code: crate boundaries, dependencies, edition, and access to the standard library.

But when you’re working with:

  • a single .rs file
  • a mixed-language repository
  • small, disposable programs (like Advent of Code)

You lose all of that context. Rust Analyzer has nothing to latch onto, and the editor experience degrades sharply.

Unlike Python, where tooling scales gracefully from one file to one thousand, Rust’s tooling assumes Cargo by default.

Motivation

Conventionally, when you start a new Rust project with cargo new <project_name>, cargo generates some configuration about your project which your Rust analyzer picks and uses to provide useful autocompletion features, go to definition support, and inline type hinting.

But when working with simpler setups like a single Rust file, you lose out on the benefits that come with the Rust analyzer and the Cargo project configuration. Unlike Programming languages like Python, which can work straightforwardly as single files and as complex project structures.
Of course, with the benefits of the autocompletion and the rest, you can still very well write and compile single file rust programs.

After stumbling into a bug while implementing a solution for the challenges in Advent of Code day 2 in Rust, and I realized how much harder it was to walkthrough the types in my program visually and get support for autocompletion, method names and signatures, I decided to do an internet search on how to configure Rust Analyzer to work for single file rust Project without Cargo.

While searching, I came across many such advice;

People kept generally hinting at using cargo, but, like in my case, it was not reasonable to set up a cargo project for every single day’s challenge, and it was a multi-language environment, and not a Rust-specific project.

In my case:

  • Each Advent of Code solution was a standalone program
  • The repository contained multiple languages
  • Creating and maintaining a Cargo project per day felt like overkill

I didn’t want a build system.
I wanted my editor to understand Rust.

Solution

Rust Analyzer has support for non-cargo based project, just like the use case I wished to use it for above, but to give Rust Analyzer details on your setup and directory to find standard Rust libraries, you have to provide these details in a rust-project.json file in the root directory containing the single Rust files you wish to work on without Cargo. See details here.

With a small amount of explicit configuration, you can give Rust Analyzer everything it needs:

  • where Rust is installed
  • which files are crates
  • which edition to use

No Cargo required.

# rust-project.json

{
  "sysroot": "/Users/Apple/.rustup/toolchains/stable-aarch64-apple-darwin",
  "crates": [
    {
      "display_name": "core",
      "root_module": "/Users/Apple/.rustup/toolchains/stable-aarch64-apple-darwin/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/core/src/lib.rs",
      "edition": "2024",
      "deps": [],
      "cfg": [
        "target_arch=\"aarch64\"",
        "target_os=\"macos\"",
        "unix"
      ],
      "env": {},
      "is_proc_macro": false
    },
    {
      "display_name": "alloc",
      "root_module": "/Users/Apple/.rustup/toolchains/stable-aarch64-apple-darwin/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/alloc/src/lib.rs",
      "edition": "2024",
      "deps": [
        { "crate": 0, "name": "core" }
      ],
      "cfg": [
        "target_arch=\"aarch64\"",
        "target_os=\"macos\"",
        "unix"
      ],
      "env": {},
      "is_proc_macro": false
    },
    {
      "display_name": "std",
      "root_module": "/Users/Apple/.rustup/toolchains/stable-aarch64-apple-darwin/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/std/src/lib.rs",
      "edition": "2024",
      "deps": [
        { "crate": 0, "name": "core" },
        { "crate": 1, "name": "alloc" }
      ],
      "cfg": [
        "target_arch=\"aarch64\"",
        "target_os=\"macos\"",
        "unix"
      ],
      "env": {},
      "is_proc_macro": false
    },
    {
      "display_name": "day_4",
      "root_module": "/Users/Apple/Documents/advent-of-codes/2025/day_4.rs",
      "edition": "2024",
      "deps": [{ "crate": 2, "name": "std" }],
      "cfg": [
        "target_arch=\"aarch64\"",
        "target_os=\"macos\"",
        "unix"
      ],
      "env": {},
      "is_proc_macro": false
    },
    {
      "display_name": "day_5",
      "root_module": "/Users/Apple/Documents/advent-of-codes/2025/day_5.rs",
      "edition": "2024",
      "deps": [{ "crate": 2, "name": "std" }],
      "cfg": [
        "target_arch=\"aarch64\"",
        "target_os=\"macos\"",
        "unix"
      ],
      "env": {},
      "is_proc_macro": false
    }
  ]
}

Explanation:

  • sysroot: Tells Rust Analyzer where your Rust toolchain lives—the standard library, core, alloc, and compiler support crates.
    You can get this value by entering the following command
rustc --print sysroot
  • crates: An array describing each logical Rust crate in the workspace.
    For simple setups, this often maps** one-to-one with a single .rs file**, but it can also represent larger module trees.
    Take note to pass the Absolute path of the root_module attribute

Notice that the first 3 crates are standard crates that Rust Analyzer needs to annotate builtin traits properly, ensure that you own defined crates (single Rust files) that depend on those traits to gain the complete type annotation benefits.

After creating and saving this file to your working directory, you should reload your editor workspace to get all the great benefits of Rust Analyzer working on your single-file Rust Programs (non-Cargo projects)

Conclusion

Rust doesn’t stop you from writing small, single-file programs, but without proper tooling, it certainly makes you feel the absence. Rust Analyzer, by default, expects Cargo to be the narrator of your project’s story, and when Cargo is missing, the editor is left guessing in the dark.

The good news is that this limitation is not a dead end. By explicitly describing your setup using a rust-project.json file, you can restore nearly all the ergonomics you’d expect from a full Cargo-based project: autocomplete, type hints, navigation, and a clearer understanding of your code’s structure.

For lightweight experiments, coding challenges, or mixed-language repositories, this approach strikes a practical balance. You keep the simplicity of single-file Rust while reclaiming the insight and confidence that come from a well-informed editor.

Sometimes, the compiler already knows enough. You just need to teach your tools to listen.

entry.title: Binding Energy: Why Iron Is the End of the Line
entry.content:
Introduction

There is a question that bothered me for a long time, and I suspect it bothers a lot of people who have read a little about nuclear energy: if you get energy by splitting heavy atoms (fission), and you also get energy by joining light atoms (fusion), how can both be true? Surely one of them has to cost energy. You can't make money by both buying and selling the same thing.

The answer turns out to be one of the most elegant ideas in physics, and it all hangs on a single graph: the binding energy curve. Once that curve makes sense, fission, fusion, why stars die, and why nobody is building iron-burning power plants all fall out of it almost for free.

This post is the foundation for a small series on nuclear physics. You don't need any background beyond high-school physics and a willingness to accept that mass and energy are the same thing.

TL;DR

  • A nucleus weighs less than the protons and neutrons it is made from. The missing mass is the binding energy, via E = mc².
  • Divide that by the number of nucleons and you get binding energy per nucleon: a measure of how tightly each particle is held.
  • That number rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks around iron and nickel (~8.8 MeV), and slowly falls for heavy nuclei.
  • Any reaction that moves nuclei towards the peak releases energy. Light nuclei climb by fusing; heavy nuclei climb by splitting. Iron is already at the top, so it can do neither.

The nucleus is lighter than its parts

Start with helium-4, the nucleus of an ordinary helium atom: two protons and two neutrons. Look up the masses (in atomic mass units, u):

ParticleMass (u)
Proton1.007276
Neutron1.008665
2 protons + 2 neutrons4.031883
Helium-4 nucleus4.001506

The assembled nucleus is lighter than its loose parts by 0.030377 u. That's not a measurement error; it's the whole story. This missing mass is called the mass defect.

Where did it go? It left as energy when the nucleus formed. Using E = mc², and the handy fact that 1 u of mass is equivalent to 931.494 MeV:

0.030377 u × 931.494 MeV/u ≈ 28.3 MeV

So 28.3 MeV of energy was released when those four nucleons snapped together, and to pull helium-4 apart again, you'd have to put those 28.3 MeV back in. That's the binding energy. It's the energy debt you'd have to repay to dismantle the nucleus.

To put "MeV" in perspective: a chemical bond, the thing that holds a molecule together and the thing we break when we burn coal or petrol, is worth a few eV. Nuclear binding energies are in the millions of eV. That factor of roughly a million is the whole reason nuclear power exists.

Binding energy per nucleon

Total binding energy grows with the size of the nucleus, which isn't very interesting on its own; of course a bigger nucleus has more glue. The useful number is the binding energy per nucleon: divide the total by the mass number A (protons + neutrons).

NucleusBinding energy per nucleon
Deuterium (²H)1.11 MeV
Helium-47.07 MeV
Carbon-127.68 MeV
Oxygen-167.98 MeV
Iron-568.79 MeV
Nickel-628.79 MeV (the actual record holder, by a hair)
Uranium-2357.59 MeV
Uranium-2387.57 MeV

Plot that for every known nucleus and you get the famous curve. In words:

 MeV per nucleon
  9 |              Fe  Ni
    |          .·'¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯``'·..
  8 |       .·'                       ``·.  U
    |     .'                              ·
  7 |   He
    |   |
    |  /
    | /
  1 |D
    +------------------------------------------- mass number A
       4      56                          235
  • A steep climb through the light elements (with helium-4 sitting conspicuously high for its size, because it is an unusually tight little package).
  • A broad peak around A ≈ 56–62: iron and nickel.
  • A slow decline all the way out to uranium and beyond.

Higher on the curve means more tightly bound, which means more stable and, crucially, lower in energy. Nature, like water, flows downhill in energy. In this graph "downhill" means "upwards on the curve". Any nuclear reaction that ends with nucleons sitting higher on this curve releases the difference as energy.

Why the curve has that shape

The shape isn't arbitrary. It comes from a tug-of-war between two forces.

The strong force: short-range glue

Protons and neutrons are held together by the strong nuclear force. It's ferociously strong, but it only reaches about one or two femtometres (about the width of a nucleon). Beyond that it falls off a cliff. So each nucleon effectively only feels its immediate neighbours.

In a tiny nucleus, most nucleons sit on the surface, with few neighbours to bond with. They're under-bonded. As the nucleus grows, a larger fraction of nucleons are buried in the interior with a full set of neighbours, so the binding per nucleon climbs. That's the steep left side of the curve.

Electromagnetism: long-range repulsion

Protons are positively charged and repel each other. Unlike the strong force, the electric force has infinite range: every proton pushes on every other proton in the nucleus, not just its neighbours.

That means the repulsion grows roughly as Z² (with Z protons) while the strong-force glue only grows roughly as A. In a small nucleus, the glue wins easily. In a big nucleus, the repulsion catches up and starts eating into the binding. That's the slow decline on the right side.

Where they balance

Somewhere around iron and nickel, the benefit of having more neighbours has mostly saturated, and the cost of proton repulsion hasn't yet become dominant. That's the peak. Iron sits at the sweet spot between "too small to be well glued" and "too big to hold its own charge together".

A model you can run: the semi-empirical mass formula

Physicists turned that intuition into an actual formula back in the 1930s. It treats the nucleus like a drop of charged liquid, which is why it's often called the liquid drop model, and it adds up five effects:

  1. Volume: every nucleon gets glue from its neighbours (proportional to A).
  2. Surface: nucleons on the surface have fewer neighbours, so subtract something proportional to the surface area, A^(2/3).
  3. Coulomb: subtract the proton–proton repulsion, roughly Z(Z−1) / A^(1/3).
  4. Asymmetry: nuclei prefer balanced numbers of protons and neutrons (a quantum effect from the Pauli exclusion principle), so subtract a penalty for imbalance, (N−Z)² / A.
  5. Pairing: nucleons like to pair up, so even–even nuclei get a small bonus and odd–odd nuclei a small penalty.

Here it is in Python:

import math

# Semi-empirical mass formula coefficients, in MeV
A_V, A_S, A_C, A_A, A_P = 15.8, 18.3, 0.714, 23.2, 12.0

def binding_energy(Z: int, A: int) -> float:
    """Approximate total binding energy of a nucleus in MeV."""
    N = A - Z
    volume = A_V * A
    surface = A_S * A ** (2 / 3)
    coulomb = A_C * Z * (Z - 1) / A ** (1 / 3)
    asymmetry = A_A * (N - Z) ** 2 / A
    if Z % 2 == 0 and N % 2 == 0:
        pairing = A_P / math.sqrt(A)
    elif Z % 2 == 1 and N % 2 == 1:
        pairing = -A_P / math.sqrt(A)
    else:
        pairing = 0.0
    return volume - surface - coulomb - asymmetry + pairing

nuclei = {
    "He-4": (2, 4),
    "C-12": (6, 12),
    "O-16": (8, 16),
    "Fe-56": (26, 56),
    "Ni-62": (28, 62),
    "U-235": (92, 235),
    "U-238": (92, 238),
}

for name, (Z, A) in nuclei.items():
    B = binding_energy(Z, A)
    print(f"{name:>7}: {B:8.1f} MeV total, {B / A:5.2f} MeV per nucleon")

Output:

   He-4:     22.2 MeV total,  5.55 MeV per nucleon
   C-12:     87.8 MeV total,  7.32 MeV per nucleon
   O-16:    123.7 MeV total,  7.73 MeV per nucleon
  Fe-56:    490.6 MeV total,  8.76 MeV per nucleon
  Ni-62:    544.6 MeV total,  8.78 MeV per nucleon
  U-235:   1790.7 MeV total,  7.62 MeV per nucleon
  U-238:   1809.5 MeV total,  7.60 MeV per nucleon

Five terms and a handful of constants, and it lands within about half a percent of reality for iron and uranium. It even finds nickel-62 slightly ahead of iron-56. I find that genuinely remarkable.

It's also honest about its limits: helium-4 comes out at 22 MeV instead of the real 28 MeV. Treating four particles as a "liquid drop" is a stretch, and helium-4 is special. Its two protons and two neutrons fill the lowest quantum shell completely, a bit like a noble gas does with electrons.
